lessons.title: V3·D1 — Transactions, atomicity and savepoints
lessons.summary: Sector 23 taught BEGIN, COMMIT and ROLLBACK. This one takes atomicity apart: the aborted state and why it exists, savepoints as real subtransactions with a real cost, deferred constraints, transactional DDL, and the fact that every single statement is already a transaction whether you asked for one or not.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·D1 — Transactions, atomicity and savepoints

Sector 23 gave you the shape: `BEGIN`, two `UPDATE`s, `COMMIT`, and the
promise that a crash in the middle leaves no half-transfer behind. That
promise is worth trusting, and most engineers stop there. This sector is
about the parts underneath it, because the parts underneath are where
production incidents live: the aborted state that swallows the rest of
your script, savepoints that quietly cost you performance at scale,
constraints that fire at the wrong moment, and the surprising truth that
you have been using transactions all along even when you never typed
`BEGIN`.

`setup.sql` gives this sector a small but deliberately awkward schema:

```sql
CREATE TABLE accounts (
  id      int PRIMARY KEY,
  owner   text NOT NULL,
  balance numeric(12,2) NOT NULL CHECK (balance >= 0)
);
-- 1 Alice 900.00, 2 Bob 100.00, 3 Escrow 0.00

CREATE TABLE ledger (
  id         bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  account_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES accounts(id),
  delta      numeric(12,2) NOT NULL,
  note       text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE seats (
  event_id int NOT NULL,
  seat_no  int NOT NULL,
  holder   text,
  CONSTRAINT seats_pk PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no)
);
-- event 1, seats 1..5, holders 'a'..'e'

CREATE TABLE import_rows (
  id      int PRIMARY KEY,
  account int NOT NULL,
  delta   numeric(12,2) NOT NULL
);
-- five rows, of which two are poison: one references a missing account,
-- one would drive a balance negative

CREATE TABLE import_rejects (
  row_id   int PRIMARY KEY,
  sqlstate text NOT NULL,
  message  text NOT NULL
);

CREATE TABLE xid_probe (step text PRIMARY KEY, xid text NOT NULL);
```

Gates run your script over an **autocommit** connection. There is no
hidden transaction wrapping your file: the `BEGIN`, `COMMIT`, `ROLLBACK`
and `SAVEPOINT` statements you write are the only transaction control in
play, exactly as if you had typed them into `psql`.

## Every statement is already a transaction

This is the sentence to internalise before anything else. When you send
`UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance * 1.1;` with no `BEGIN`, the server
opens a transaction, runs the statement, and commits — an *implicit*
transaction. That is why a single `UPDATE` that touches four million rows
and violates a `CHECK` on the last one changes nothing at all. People
reach for `BEGIN` around one statement for safety; it buys them nothing.
`BEGIN` buys you two things and only two: the ability to make **several**
statements atomic, and the ability to look at your own uncommitted work
before deciding whether the world should see it.

## The aborted state

```
ERROR:  division by zero
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of
        transaction block
```

The second error is the one that confuses people. After *any* error
inside an explicit transaction, PostgreSQL refuses everything except
`ROLLBACK`, `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`, and `COMMIT` (which is treated as a
rollback and tells you so). It is not being difficult. The alternative —
letting you keep going after a failed statement — is what MySQL does, and
it means a transaction can commit having silently skipped a step. Postgres
would rather stop the world than hand you a partially-applied unit of
work.

The practical consequence is that your error handling is part of your
transaction design. A driver that catches an exception, logs it, and
carries on issuing statements on the same connection will produce a
cascade of "current transaction is aborted" errors that bury the real one.
Every mature client library either rolls back automatically or marks the
connection dirty.

## Savepoints are subtransactions, and they are not free

`SAVEPOINT s` opens a **subtransaction**. `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s`
discards everything since, returns the transaction to a usable state, and
— importantly — leaves the savepoint in place so you can roll back to it
again. `RELEASE SAVEPOINT s` forgets the savepoint and merges its work
into the parent; it is not a commit, and the work still disappears if the
outer transaction rolls back.

The cost is real. Each subtransaction that actually writes gets its own
transaction id. A backend caches 64 of them; past that it *overflows*, and
every other backend checking visibility of your rows has to consult
`pg_subtrans` on disk instead of a cached array. A loop that wraps each of
50,000 rows in its own savepoint is the classic way to make an entire
cluster mysteriously slow — the symptom shows up in
`pg_stat_activity.backend_xid` versus `backend_xmin`, and in
`SubtransSLRU` wait events, nowhere near the code that caused it.

PL/pgSQL's `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN ... END` block is a savepoint with
different syntax. A trigger or function with an exception handler in a
per-row loop has exactly the same cost, which is why "just add an
exception block" is not a free way to make a batch tolerant.

## Constraints have timing

A `CHECK` is evaluated per row, immediately. A `UNIQUE` or `PRIMARY KEY`
is enforced at statement end by default but *can* be deferred; a foreign
key is deferrable too. `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` plus
`SET CONSTRAINTS ... DEFERRED` inside a transaction moves the check to
commit time, which is the only sane way to swap two rows that share a
unique key, or to insert a parent and child in whatever order your ORM
produced. Note the asymmetry: `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` are **never**
deferrable in PostgreSQL. If you find yourself wanting a deferred `CHECK`,
you actually want a constraint trigger.

## Transactional DDL

`CREATE TABLE`, `ALTER TABLE`, `DROP INDEX`, even `CREATE TYPE` — all
transactional. A migration that creates a table, backfills it, adds a
constraint and fails on the constraint leaves the database exactly as it
started. MySQL and Oracle cannot do this, which is why their migration
tooling is full of manual rollback scripts. Two exceptions worth
memorising: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `VACUUM` cannot run inside a
transaction block, and `CREATE DATABASE` cannot either.

## What the eight missions cover

You will write a guarded transfer that refuses to overdraw; drive a
transaction into the aborted state and recover it; use a savepoint to skip
one poison row in a batch without losing the batch; see what `RELEASE`
really does; defer a unique constraint to swap two seats; roll back a DDL
migration; measure the subtransaction cost of an exception handler in a
loop; and prove that a single statement is atomic without any `BEGIN` at
all. The challenge builds a real importer. The review re-approaches
atomicity from the direction of a job that must be safe to run twice.

# Reading - sql/v3d01_transaction_atomicity

Atomicity is usually taught as a guarantee you receive. It is more useful
to think of it as a *boundary you draw*, because the guarantee is
automatic and the boundary is a design decision that people get wrong
constantly.

## Notes

**The unit of atomicity is the thing you should be arguing about.** Wrap
too little and you get the torn transfer. Wrap too much and you hold locks
and an old snapshot across an HTTP call to a payment provider, which is
sector D8's entire subject. The right boundary is "the smallest set of
writes that must be true together", and the tell that you have it wrong is
usually a network call or a sleep between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`.

**`ROLLBACK` is not only error handling.** Between `BEGIN` and the end of
the transaction your changes are real to you and invisible to everyone
else. That makes a transaction a *place to try things*: run the delete,
count what is left, and roll back if the count is wrong. Engineers who
have this habit rarely destroy production data; engineers who type
destructive statements in autocommit eventually do.

**The aborted state is a feature with a sharp edge.** `COMMIT` on an
aborted transaction does not raise an error — it returns `ROLLBACK` as its
command tag and quietly throws your work away. Code that does
`try: work() finally: conn.commit()` therefore *looks* successful in the
logs while having committed nothing. Check the command tag or, better, let
your driver's context manager decide.

**Savepoint semantics are asymmetric.** `ROLLBACK TO s` keeps `s` alive;
you may roll back to it repeatedly, which is exactly what a retry loop
wants. `RELEASE s` destroys it and everything nested inside it, but keeps
the *work*. Neither one commits anything. A common bug is releasing a
savepoint and believing the record is now safe — it is safe only from
`ROLLBACK TO`, not from the outer transaction failing.

**Deferred constraints move the failure, they do not remove it.** With
`SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED`, a duplicate key raises at `COMMIT`. That
means the error arrives at a point in your code with no context about
which statement caused it, so defer narrowly — name the constraint rather
than using `ALL` — and only for the transaction that needs it.

**Read-only transactions still matter.** `BEGIN READ ONLY` (or
`SET TRANSACTION READ ONLY`) makes an accidental write impossible and
documents intent to the next reader of the code. `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL
REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` additionally waits until it can
guarantee a snapshot with no serialization failures — the correct
incantation for a long analytics query on a serializable system.

## ex1 — the guarded transfer

The `CHECK (balance >= 0)` will stop an overdraw with an error, but an
error is a poor user experience and a poorer log line. Putting the guard
in the `WHERE` clause — `WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 250` — turns the
failure into an updated row count of zero, which your application can
inspect and turn into a real message. The transaction is still what makes
the pair atomic; the guard is what makes the failure legible.

## ex2 — recovering from the aborted state

The gate injects a failing statement mid-script. Your remainder gets
exactly one useful option. Notice that the debit you already issued
evaporates without you undoing it by hand — that is the whole point, and
it is why "compensating updates" written in application code are almost
always a sign that someone did not trust the transaction.

## ex3 — one poison row, not one lost batch

`import_rows` contains two rows that cannot be applied. Without
savepoints, the first one aborts the transaction and the other four
records are lost. With a savepoint taken before each row and rolled back
on failure, you apply three and record two rejects. This is the shape of
every real importer.

## ex4 — RELEASE versus ROLLBACK TO

Worth doing slowly. After `RELEASE`, the name is gone; a later
`ROLLBACK TO` on it raises `savepoint "s" does not exist`. But the rows
written inside it are still there, still uncommitted, still doomed if the
outer transaction rolls back.

## ex5 — swapping two seats

Seat 2 must become seat 3 and vice versa, under a primary key on
`(event_id, seat_no)`. Immediate checking makes the first `UPDATE` fail
against a row that is about to move out of the way. Deferring the
constraint to commit time makes the intermediate state legal. The
alternative dance — park one row on seat 999, move the other, move it
back — works, is three statements instead of two, and is what people write
when they do not know constraints have timing.

## ex6 — a migration that changes its mind

Create a table, insert into it, then roll back, and prove with
`to_regclass` that nothing survives. Cherish it: this is the property that
makes PostgreSQL migrations safe to run without a manual undo file.

## ex7 — the price of an exception handler

A `DO` block with a per-row exception handler versus one without.
`pg_current_xact_id()` at the start and end shows the outer id unchanged
while the subtransaction counter climbs. The lesson is not "never use
exception handlers" — it is "know that each one is a subtransaction, and
do not put one inside a loop over a million rows".

## ex8 — atomicity without BEGIN

One `UPDATE` over all three accounts, where the last row evaluated would
violate the `CHECK`. Nothing changes. No `BEGIN` was typed. Implicit
transactions are the reason people can go years without understanding
transactions and mostly get away with it.

## Further reading

- [SQL: BEGIN / COMMIT / ROLLBACK](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-begin.html) — including `AND CHAIN`, which starts a fresh transaction with the same characteristics.
- [SAVEPOINT](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-savepoint.html) — and the note that repeated `SAVEPOINT` with the same name nests rather than replaces.
- [SET CONSTRAINTS](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-set-constraints.html) — deferral, and which constraint types can be deferred at all.
- [Subtransactions and performance](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — plus the `pg_subtrans` discussion in the source's `README.tuplock`.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·D1 — Transactions, atomicity and savepoints (archive)

The deep version of the sector. Read it once now and again the week you
first meet "current transaction is aborted" in a production log.

## Concepts

### The four statements

```sql
BEGIN;                      -- or START TRANSACTION
  ...
COMMIT;                     -- make it visible, durably
ROLLBACK;                   -- discard it
SAVEPOINT s;                -- open a subtransaction
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;    -- discard back to s, keep the transaction
RELEASE SAVEPOINT s;        -- forget s, keep its work
```

`BEGIN` accepts characteristics inline, which is the tidiest way to set
them:

```sql
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY DEFERRABLE;
```

`COMMIT AND CHAIN` / `ROLLBACK AND CHAIN` end the transaction and
immediately start another with the same characteristics — useful in a
script that processes batches with identical settings.

### Implicit transactions

Every statement outside an explicit block runs in its own transaction.
This is why the following is already atomic:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 100 WHERE id IN (1, 2, 3);
```

If row 3 violates `CHECK (balance >= 0)`, rows 1 and 2 are not changed.
The only thing `BEGIN` would add here is the ability to look before
committing.

### The aborted state, precisely

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (1, -10, 'ok');
SELECT 1/0;                    -- ERROR: division by zero
SELECT count(*) FROM ledger;   -- ERROR: current transaction is aborted
ROLLBACK;                      -- the only way out (or ROLLBACK TO)
```

`COMMIT` here does not error. It returns the command tag `ROLLBACK`. Code
that treats "no exception from commit" as "the work landed" is wrong on
this path, and it is a genuinely common production bug.

### Savepoints as a batch strategy

```sql
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT row_1;
  INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (999, 5, 'bad fk');
-- ERROR: violates foreign key constraint
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT row_1;   -- transaction is usable again
  INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (1, 5, 'good');
COMMIT;
```

In PL/pgSQL the same thing is spelled with an exception block:

```sql
DO $$
DECLARE r record; ok int := 0; bad int := 0;
BEGIN
  FOR r IN SELECT * FROM import_rows ORDER BY id LOOP
    BEGIN
      UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + r.delta WHERE id = r.account;
      IF NOT FOUND THEN RAISE EXCEPTION 'no account %', r.account; END IF;
      ok := ok + 1;
    EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
      bad := bad + 1;
    END;
  END LOOP;
  RAISE NOTICE 'applied % rejected %', ok, bad;
END $$;
```

That inner `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END` **is** a savepoint. It is the
reason the loop can continue after a constraint violation, and it is the
reason the loop is measurably slower than one without a handler.

### Deferred constraints

```sql
ALTER TABLE seats DROP CONSTRAINT seats_pk;
ALTER TABLE seats ADD CONSTRAINT seats_pk
  PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE;

BEGIN;
  SET CONSTRAINTS seats_pk DEFERRED;
  UPDATE seats SET seat_no = 3 WHERE event_id = 1 AND seat_no = 2;
  UPDATE seats SET seat_no = 2 WHERE event_id = 1 AND seat_no = 3
    AND holder = 'c';
COMMIT;                        -- the check happens here
```

Two details people trip on. `INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` still requires the
constraint to be declared `DEFERRABLE`; you cannot defer a constraint that
was not created deferrable, and altering it means rebuilding the index.
And a deferrable unique constraint cannot be used as the arbiter of an
`ON CONFLICT` clause — a fact that sector D6 will make you care about.

### Watching a transaction from outside

Everything above is observable while it happens:

```sql
SELECT pid,
       state,                      -- 'active' or 'idle in transaction'
       backend_xid,                -- the write id, NULL if read-only
       backend_xmin,               -- the oldest xid this backend's snapshot needs
       now() - xact_start AS txn_age,
       left(query, 60) AS q
  FROM pg_stat_activity
 WHERE backend_type = 'client backend'
   AND xact_start IS NOT NULL
 ORDER BY xact_start;
```

`state = 'idle in transaction'` with a growing `txn_age` is the shape of
every incident in sector D8. `backend_xid IS NULL` with a non-null
`backend_xmin` means a read-only transaction that has still pinned the
horizon. And a `pg_prepared_xacts` row you did not expect means somebody
called `PREPARE TRANSACTION` and never resolved it.

## Common mistakes

1. **Wrapping one statement in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT` "for safety".** It is
   already atomic. You added a round trip and a longer-held snapshot.
2. **Catching an exception and continuing on the same connection.** Every
   subsequent statement fails with "current transaction is aborted" and
   your log fills with the wrong error.
3. **Trusting `COMMIT` not to raise.** On an aborted transaction it does
   not raise; it rolls back and says so in the command tag.
4. **A savepoint per row in a large loop.** Fine for hundreds of rows,
   pathological for hundreds of thousands: subtransaction id overflow past
   64 pushes every other backend into `pg_subtrans` lookups.
5. **`SET CONSTRAINTS ALL DEFERRED` as a default.** Now every violation
   surfaces at commit with no statement context.
6. **Expecting a deferred `CHECK`.** `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` are never
   deferrable. Use a `CONSTRAINT TRIGGER ... DEFERRABLE INITIALLY
   DEFERRED` if you truly need end-of-transaction validation.
7. **Holding a transaction open across a network call.** Sector D8's
   subject, and the single most expensive habit in this list.
8. **Assuming DDL rollback works everywhere.** It does in PostgreSQL; the
   migration you ported from MySQL may be full of hand-written undo steps
   you no longer need — and `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` still cannot join
   the party.

## The interview answer

> *"What does atomicity actually guarantee, and where does it stop?"*

Atomicity guarantees that the statements between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`
become visible to other transactions all at once, or not at all — there is
no observable intermediate state, and a crash at any point leaves the
prior state. It does **not** guarantee isolation from concurrent writers
(that is the isolation level, and PostgreSQL's default `READ COMMITTED`
allows plenty), it does not guarantee your transaction will succeed, and
it does not extend past the database: an email sent inside a transaction
that later rolls back has still been sent. In PostgreSQL the mechanism is
that the commit record's arrival in `pg_xact` is what flips every row
version written by that transaction from invisible to visible at once, so
atomicity falls out of a single-bit change rather than any undo work.
Savepoints refine the boundary by creating subtransactions with their own
ids, at a cost that becomes visible past 64 per backend.

## Check yourself

1. Why does PostgreSQL refuse further statements after an error inside a
   transaction, and what does MySQL do instead?
2. What command tag does `COMMIT` return on an aborted transaction?
3. After `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s`, does `s` still exist? After
   `RELEASE SAVEPOINT s`?
4. Name two constraint types that can never be deferred.
5. What is the observable symptom, on *other* backends, of one backend
   opening thousands of subtransactions?
6. Give one statement that cannot run inside a transaction block, and say
   why.
7. Why is `WHERE id = 1 AND balance >= 250` often better than relying on
   the `CHECK` constraint to stop an overdraw?
8. You wrap a single `UPDATE` in `BEGIN`/`COMMIT`. What did you gain?
9. A colleague's importer uses a PL/pgSQL exception handler per row and is
   slow. What is the mechanism, and what would you measure?
10. How do you swap two rows that share a unique key, in two statements?
11. What does `BEGIN READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` wait for, and why would you
    want it?
12. Your migration adds a column, backfills it, and adds a `NOT NULL`
    that fails. What state is the database in?
13. Why can a deferrable unique constraint not be used as an
    `ON CONFLICT` arbiter?
14. An email is sent inside a transaction that rolls back. What did
    atomicity do for you?

# Long read — what a commit actually is

The mental model most people carry for transactions comes from bank
account examples, and it is a model of *undo*: you make changes, and if
something goes wrong the database puts them back. That model is wrong for
PostgreSQL in an interesting way, and getting the right one makes every
other topic in this volume easier.

## There is no undo log

PostgreSQL does not maintain a rollback segment. When you `UPDATE` a row,
the old version stays exactly where it was and a new version is written
elsewhere, tagged with your transaction id in its `xmin` field. When you
`DELETE`, nothing is removed; the existing version gets your transaction
id in its `xmax`. Your writes are physically present in the table's pages
the moment you make them — before you commit, before anyone has agreed
they should exist.

What makes them invisible is not their location but the *status* of your
transaction id, which lives in a separate structure, `pg_xact` (once
called `pg_clog`), holding two bits per transaction: in progress,
committed, or aborted. A reader deciding whether it can see a row version
looks at `xmin`, asks whether that transaction committed, and compares it
against its own snapshot.

So `COMMIT` is, at heart, one bit changing from "in progress" to
"committed", plus the durable write-ahead log record that makes that
change survive a crash. Every row version your transaction wrote flips
from invisible to visible simultaneously, because they all point at the
same status bit. Atomicity is not implemented; it is a consequence of the
representation.

`ROLLBACK` is even cheaper: mark the transaction aborted and walk away.
The rows you wrote are garbage now, and `VACUUM` will reclaim them later.
This is why aborting a transaction in PostgreSQL is nearly instantaneous
regardless of how much it wrote, and why Oracle, which really does keep an
undo log, has the opposite performance profile — cheap reads of old data,
expensive rollbacks. It is also why a workload with a high abort rate is a
workload that generates bloat, which is sector D2's territory.

## Where subtransactions come from

If atomicity is one status bit per transaction id, a savepoint needs its
own id — otherwise there would be no way to make *some* of a transaction's
writes disappear while keeping the rest. That is exactly what happens: the
first write after `SAVEPOINT s` acquires a new transaction id, a child of
the current one, and `pg_subtrans` records the parent link. Visibility
checks for a subtransaction's rows must therefore resolve the chain to the
top-level transaction and then read its status.

The performance story follows directly. Each backend keeps a cache of up
to `PGPROC_MAX_CACHED_SUBXIDS` (64) child ids in shared memory, so other
backends can answer "is this subxid part of an in-progress transaction?"
without touching disk. Open a 65th, and the backend's entry is marked
*overflowed*. From that moment, every other backend performing a
visibility check against your rows may have to read `pg_subtrans` — an
SLRU with a small, fixed-size cache. On a busy system this shows up as
`LWLock:SubtransSLRU` wait events across the whole cluster, caused by one
job nobody was looking at. The reports of this from Cloudflare and others
have made "savepoint per row" a well-known antipattern, and it is why
PostgreSQL 17 made the SLRU cache sizes configurable
(`subtransaction_buffers`) rather than fixed.

Note also that PL/pgSQL exception handlers are subtransactions, so an
`EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS` inside a `FOR` loop over a large table has this
cost even though no savepoint appears in the source.

## The durable half of commit

Atomicity is the status bit; durability is the write-ahead log. Before any
change reaches a data page on disk, a record describing it is appended to
the WAL, and `COMMIT` is not allowed to return until the WAL up to and
including the commit record has been flushed. That flush is an `fsync`,
and an `fsync` is the slowest thing a commit does — typically far slower
than the work the transaction performed.

Two knobs follow from this, and both are frequently misused. `commit_delay`
asks a committing backend to pause briefly so that other backends
committing at the same moment can share one flush; it helps only under
genuine concurrency and hurts everything else. `synchronous_commit = off`
lets `COMMIT` return before the flush, trading a bounded window of recent
transactions (up to `wal_writer_delay` times three) for a large throughput
win. It is *not* a corruption risk — the database still recovers to a
consistent state — but it is a data-loss risk, and the distinction is
worth being precise about in a design review. It can also be set per
transaction with `SET LOCAL synchronous_commit = off`, which is the right
granularity: durable for payments, relaxed for the analytics event table.

The fsync cost is also the real argument for batching. Ten thousand
single-row inserts in autocommit are ten thousand flushes. The same rows
in one transaction are one. That is usually a hundredfold difference, and
it explains why "the import is slow" is so often solved by a `BEGIN` in
the right place rather than by an index.

## Two-phase commit, and why you probably should not

`PREPARE TRANSACTION 'id'` splits `COMMIT` in two: the transaction becomes
durable and its locks are held, but its status stays in limbo until some
process issues `COMMIT PREPARED` or `ROLLBACK PREPARED`. It exists for
distributed transaction managers coordinating PostgreSQL with another
resource manager.

The reason `max_prepared_transactions` defaults to zero is that a prepared
transaction that nobody resolves is a permanent hazard: it holds its
locks, and it holds back the xmin horizon, forever, surviving restarts.
An orphaned prepared transaction is one of the very few ways to make a
PostgreSQL cluster genuinely stuck, and it will not clear on its own. Use
it if you are implementing a transaction manager. Otherwise, reach for the
outbox pattern — write the intent to a table in the same local
transaction, and have a separate process deliver it — which gives you
atomicity where it matters without a distributed protocol.

## When not to use a transaction

Explicit transactions are cheap but not free, and there are shapes where
they are the wrong tool.

**Around a single statement.** Already atomic. You added latency.

**Around a long-running read on a busy system.** Your snapshot pins the
xmin horizon, `VACUUM` cannot remove any row version newer than it, and
tables bloat cluster-wide. `REPEATABLE READ READ ONLY DEFERRABLE` at least
makes the intent explicit, but the horizon cost is the same. If you need a
consistent long read, take an exported snapshot or read from a replica.

**Around anything that talks to the network.** Charging a card inside a
transaction means the row locks and the snapshot are held for the duration
of somebody else's outage. The correct shape is: short transaction to
record intent, network call outside, short transaction to record the
outcome, idempotency key so the retry is safe. Sector D6 builds that key
and sector D8 shows the pool exhaustion that the naive version causes.

**For "batch it all up so it is faster".** Grouping ten thousand inserts
into one transaction genuinely is faster than ten thousand implicit
transactions, because each commit is an fsync. Grouping ten million is
slower and riskier: a failure at 99% redoes everything, the locks are held
longer, and the `xmin` horizon problem returns. Batches of a few thousand,
committed as you go, are the shape that survives contact with production.

## Historical note

The `SAVEPOINT` and nested-transaction machinery arrived in PostgreSQL 8.0
(2005), the same release that made Windows a first-class platform. Before
that, an error genuinely did doom your whole transaction with no recourse,
and the workaround was to run each statement in autocommit and reimplement
compensation by hand — which is precisely the pattern you still find,
fossilised, in application code written against that era's databases.
Transactional DDL, by contrast, has been there essentially forever, and
remains one of the strongest practical arguments for PostgreSQL over its
peers: it is the difference between a migration that fails and a migration
that fails *halfway*.

## Exercise 1 — the transfer that refuses to overdraw

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Treasury wants two transfers attempted in one
transaction:

1. **250.00 from Alice (id 1) to Bob (id 2)** — this one must happen.
2. **5000.00 from Alice to Bob** — Alice cannot cover it. This one must
   change nothing **and must not raise an error**. A failed transfer is a
   business outcome, not a crash.

Relying on `CHECK (balance >= 0)` to stop the second transfer would abort
the transaction and lose the first one. Put the guard in the `WHERE`
clause instead, and make the credit conditional on the debit having
actually happened — a data-modifying CTE lets you express "credit only if
the debit returned a row" in a single statement:

```sql
WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE t SET ... WHERE id = 1 AND <guard> RETURNING id
)
UPDATE t SET ... WHERE id = 2 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM debit);
```

Every successful leg must also write to `ledger`: one row for the debit
(negative `delta`) and one for the credit (positive), both with the note
`'transfer'`.

Final state the gate checks: Alice 650.00, Bob 350.00, Escrow 0.00, and
exactly two `ledger` rows.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
There are two failure models available to you. One raises an error and
poisons the whole transaction; the other returns "zero rows updated" and
lets you carry on. Which clause turns the first into the second?

## Hint 2
A data-modifying CTE runs its sub-statements exactly once, and later parts
of the same statement can read what they returned:

```sql
WITH gone AS (
  DELETE FROM staging WHERE ready RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO archive (id) SELECT id FROM gone;
```

Nothing in `gone` means nothing inserted — no `IF` needed.

## Hint 3
Write one statement per transfer. Each is a `WITH debit AS (UPDATE ...
RETURNING ...), credit AS (UPDATE ... WHERE ... EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM
debit) RETURNING ...) INSERT INTO ledger ... SELECT ... FROM debit UNION
ALL SELECT ... FROM credit`. On the 5000 attempt every CTE yields zero
rows, so the insert writes nothing. Wrap both statements in `BEGIN` /
`COMMIT`.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Start from the end: after the script, `ledger` must hold exactly two rows.
That number tells you the ledger insert has to be driven by what the
updates actually did, not by a literal `VALUES` list.

## Hint 2
`EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM debit)` inside an `UPDATE`'s `WHERE` is legal and
is evaluated once. Compare with the wrong shape:

```sql
UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + 250 WHERE id = 2;  -- unconditional
```

This credits Bob even when Alice was too poor to pay, and no error tells
you.

## Hint 3
`INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) SELECT 1, -250.00,
'transfer' FROM debit UNION ALL SELECT 2, 250.00, 'transfer' FROM credit`
gives you exactly one row per leg that actually moved money, and zero rows
when neither did. The `numeric` literals should carry two decimals to
match the column's scale.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3d01_transaction_atomicity / ex1 — guarded transfers that fail quietly
BEGIN;

-- Transfer 1: 250.00 from Alice to Bob. Alice has 900.00, so it applies.
WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE accounts
     SET balance = balance - 250.00
   WHERE id = 1
     AND balance >= 250.00
  RETURNING id
), credit AS (
  UPDATE accounts
     SET balance = balance + 250.00
   WHERE id = 2
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM debit)
  RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note)
SELECT 1, -250.00, 'transfer' FROM debit
UNION ALL
SELECT 2,  250.00, 'transfer' FROM credit;

-- Transfer 2: 5000.00 from Alice to Bob. The guard fails, so every CTE
-- returns zero rows: no update, no ledger entry, and no error.
WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE accounts
     SET balance = balance - 5000.00
   WHERE id = 1
     AND balance >= 5000.00
  RETURNING id
), credit AS (
  UPDATE accounts
     SET balance = balance + 5000.00
   WHERE id = 2
     AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM debit)
  RETURNING id
)
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note)
SELECT 1, -5000.00, 'transfer' FROM debit
UNION ALL
SELECT 2,  5000.00, 'transfer' FROM credit;

COMMIT;

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — the aborted state, and the only way out

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. Operations begins moving **600.00 from Alice (id
1) into Escrow (id 3)** and the process dies between the debit and the
credit.

Your script must contain this exact line, on its own, between the debit
and the rest:

```
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
```

The gate splits your file at that marker, runs the first half on one
connection, injects a crashing statement (`SELECT 1/0`), then sends your
remainder down the *same* connection. At that moment the transaction is in
the aborted state: PostgreSQL will reject every statement except
`ROLLBACK`, `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT`, and `COMMIT` (which rolls back and
says so).

Shape of the file:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...;                 -- the debit
INSERT INTO ledger ...;     -- the debit's ledger row
-- INJECT FAILURE HERE
<your recovery>
```

The gate then checks Alice is still 900.00, Escrow still 0.00, and
`ledger` is empty. Do not put a `SELECT` after the marker to "check
things" — it will fail with `25P02` and take your recovery down with it.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
You do not have to undo the debit. Ask instead: what is the smallest thing
you can say to the server that makes the half-finished work cease to
exist?

## Hint 2
The error message names its own cure:

```
ERROR:  current transaction is aborted, commands ignored until end of
        transaction block
```

"End of transaction block" is a phrase with exactly two spellings in SQL,
and only one of them discards the work.

## Hint 3
The remainder after the marker is a single statement. `COMMIT` would also
end the block, and would also discard everything — but it reports the
command tag `ROLLBACK`, which is a terrible thing to find in a log. Say
what you mean.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Try the wrong version first, locally: put `SELECT count(*) FROM ledger;`
after the marker and read the SQLSTATE you get. Understanding why that
fails is the whole exercise.

## Hint 2
Compare with the savepoint form you will meet in ex4:

```sql
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT s;
SELECT 1/0;                   -- boom
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;      -- accepted even while aborted
SELECT 'still alive';         -- works again
```

`ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT` is the other statement the aborted state accepts.
Here you have no savepoint, so you have one option left.

## Hint 3
One word, one semicolon. Everything the first half wrote — the balance
change and the ledger row — disappears because it was never visible to
anyone else in the first place.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — one poison row must not cost you the batch

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. `import_rows` holds five records to apply to
`accounts`:

| id | account | delta    | outcome                                  |
|---:|--------:|---------:|------------------------------------------|
| 1  | 1       |  -50.00  | applies                                  |
| 2  | 999     |   25.00  | no such account                          |
| 3  | 2       |   40.00  | applies                                  |
| 4  | 1       | -5000.00 | would drive Alice below zero (`CHECK`)   |
| 5  | 3       |   10.00  | applies                                  |

Write an importer that applies every row it can, rejects the two it
cannot, and does not abandon the batch. For each row:

- `UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance + delta WHERE id = account`. If
  no row was updated, that record is a reject — raise so the handler sees
  it.
- On success also `INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note)` with the
  note `'import ' || id`.
- On failure insert into `import_rejects (row_id, sqlstate, message)`.

A plain script cannot do this: the first failure poisons the transaction.
You need a savepoint per record. In PL/pgSQL that is spelled as a nested
`BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN ... END` block — the exception
handler *is* a savepoint, which is the point of the exercise. Write it as
a single `DO $$ ... $$;` block; a `DO` block is one statement, so the
whole import is atomic without you typing `BEGIN`.

Final state: Alice 850.00, Bob 140.00, Escrow 10.00, three `ledger` rows,
two `import_rejects` rows (ids 2 and 4).

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Order matters here in a way that is easy to miss: row 4 fails *because*
row 1 already succeeded. Process the rows by `id` ascending so the
arithmetic matches the table above.

## Hint 2
The skeleton of a per-row recovery loop:

```sql
FOR r IN SELECT * FROM src ORDER BY id LOOP
  BEGIN
    ...work...
  EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
    ...record the failure...
  END;
END LOOP;
```

Inside the handler, `SQLSTATE` and `SQLERRM` are in scope and describe
what just went wrong.

## Hint 3
"No such account" produces no error by itself — `UPDATE ... WHERE id =
999` simply reports zero rows. Check `IF NOT FOUND THEN RAISE EXCEPTION
...` right after the update so that case reaches the same handler as the
`CHECK` violation. Everything the failed record wrote is already gone by
the time your handler runs; the insert into `import_rejects` happens in a
healthy transaction.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what state the transaction is in *inside* the `EXCEPTION` branch.
PL/pgSQL rolled back to the block's implicit savepoint before entering the
handler, so you are allowed to write. That is why recording the reject
works at all.

## Hint 2
`WHEN OTHERS` catches broadly. If you want to see the two failures are
genuinely different, catch them separately:

```sql
EXCEPTION
  WHEN check_violation THEN ...
  WHEN OTHERS THEN ...
```

`23514` is the `CHECK` violation; your own `RAISE EXCEPTION` defaults to
`P0001`.

## Hint 3
Declare `r record` and two counters, loop `FOR r IN SELECT * FROM
import_rows ORDER BY id`, and end with a `RAISE NOTICE` reporting applied
and rejected counts. The gate reads the tables, not the notice, but the
notice is what you would actually want in a real job's log.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — savepoints nest, and RELEASE is not a commit

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. This one is a prediction exercise: write the
script, decide what survives, then run it.

Reusing a savepoint name does not replace the old savepoint — it creates a
second one that *hides* the first. `ROLLBACK TO` reaches the innermost
savepoint with that name and leaves it in place. `RELEASE` destroys the
innermost one, keeping its work, and uncovers the outer one.

Write exactly this transaction against `ledger` (every insert uses
`account_id` 1 and `delta` 0.00; only the note differs):

1. `BEGIN`
2. insert note `'a'`
3. `SAVEPOINT s`
4. insert note `'b'`
5. `SAVEPOINT s` — the same name again
6. insert note `'c'`
7. `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s`
8. insert note `'d'`
9. `RELEASE SAVEPOINT s`
10. `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s`
11. insert note `'e'`
12. `COMMIT`

Before running it, write down which notes you expect to survive. The gate
checks the exact set.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Draw a stack. Step 3 pushes an `s`. Step 5 pushes another `s` on top.
Which one does a `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s` at step 7 find?

## Hint 2
Two rules do all the work:

- `ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s` discards work done after `s` **and keeps `s`
  on the stack**, so you can roll back to it again.
- `RELEASE SAVEPOINT s` pops `s` **and keeps the work done after it**.

Step 9 therefore keeps `'d'` but uncovers the outer `s` from step 3.

## Hint 3
Step 10 rolls back to the savepoint taken *before* `'b'` was written, so
`'b'` and `'d'` both go. Two notes survive to `COMMIT`. If you predicted
three, you assumed `RELEASE` made `'d'` permanent — it only made it safe
from a rollback to the savepoint that no longer exists.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what `RELEASE` would have to mean for `'d'` to be safe. It would have
to be a commit — and a commit of part of a transaction is precisely the
thing atomicity forbids.

## Hint 2
Verify your stack model on a smaller case first:

```sql
BEGIN;
SAVEPOINT s; SAVEPOINT s;
RELEASE SAVEPOINT s;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;   -- succeeds: the outer s is still there
RELEASE SAVEPOINT s;
ROLLBACK TO SAVEPOINT s;   -- ERROR: savepoint "s" does not exist
ROLLBACK;
```

## Hint 3
Your file is twelve lines of straight-line SQL with no branching. The
whole difficulty is in the prediction, so write the prediction as a
comment at the top before you run it, and leave it there — it is the part
of the exercise you will still remember in a year.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — swapping two rows under a primary key

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Event 1 has seats 1–5 held by `'a'`–`'e'`.
Customer service must **swap seats 2 and 3**: after your script, seat 2 is
held by `'c'` and seat 3 by `'b'`. Everything else is unchanged.

`seats_pk` is `PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no)` and it is checked
immediately, so the obvious two updates collide: the first one produces
two rows with `seat_no = 3` and the statement fails with `23505`.

The park-it-on-seat-999 trick works and is what people write. Do the real
thing instead: make the constraint deferrable and defer it for this
transaction only, so the intermediate duplicate is legal and uniqueness is
verified at `COMMIT`.

Three facts you need:

- A constraint can only be deferred if it was created `DEFERRABLE`. Ours
  was not, so you must drop and re-add it — inside the same transaction,
  because DDL is transactional here.
- `DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE` keeps the everyday behaviour and lets a
  transaction opt in with `SET CONSTRAINTS <name> DEFERRED`.
- Re-add it with the same name, `seats_pk`, so the schema is unchanged
  afterwards apart from its deferrability.

The gate checks the two holders swapped, that no other seat moved, and
that `seats_pk` still exists as a primary key.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The constraint is not wrong; its *timing* is. Ask when the uniqueness of
`(event_id, seat_no)` actually has to be true — after every statement, or
only when someone else can see the table?

## Hint 2
The opt-in is a session/transaction-scoped statement, not part of the
`UPDATE`:

```sql
BEGIN;
  SET CONSTRAINTS my_fk DEFERRED;
  INSERT INTO child ...;   -- parent does not exist yet
  INSERT INTO parent ...;  -- now it does
COMMIT;                    -- the FK is checked here
```

## Hint 3
Four statements between `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`: drop the constraint, add it
back as `PRIMARY KEY (event_id, seat_no) DEFERRABLE INITIALLY IMMEDIATE`,
`SET CONSTRAINTS seats_pk DEFERRED`, then the two updates. Give the second
update a `holder = 'c'` predicate — after the first update two rows have
`seat_no = 3`, and you only want to move one of them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Write the naive two-update version first and read the error. `23505` on
`seats_pk` with a detail line naming `(1, 3)` tells you exactly which
moment in the transaction the database objected to.

## Hint 2
Note what is *not* available: `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` can never be
deferred, only `UNIQUE`, `PRIMARY KEY`, `EXCLUDE` and `FOREIGN KEY`. If
this had been a `CHECK (seat_no BETWEEN 1 AND 5)` problem, the answer
would have been a deferred constraint trigger instead.

## Hint 3
After the first `UPDATE` moves `'b'` to seat 3, the table momentarily
holds `(1,3,'b')` and `(1,3,'c')`. Your second `UPDATE` must identify the
one to move by `holder`, not by `seat_no` alone, or it will move both rows
to seat 2 and fail at commit — with the failure arriving at `COMMIT`,
which is exactly the debugging cost of deferring.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — a migration that changes its mind

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. This is the property that makes PostgreSQL
migrations safe to run without a hand-written undo file, and it is worth
proving to yourself once.

Write a transaction that performs a plausible migration and then abandons
it:

1. `BEGIN`
2. `CREATE TABLE fee_schedule (tier int PRIMARY KEY, pct numeric(5,4) NOT
   NULL)`
3. insert tiers `(1, 0.0100)` and `(2, 0.0250)`
4. `ALTER TABLE accounts ADD COLUMN fee_tier int NOT NULL DEFAULT 1`
5. `ALTER TABLE accounts ADD CONSTRAINT accounts_fee_tier_fkey FOREIGN KEY
   (fee_tier) REFERENCES fee_schedule(tier)`
6. `ROLLBACK`

Then, **after** the rollback, one final `SELECT` returning a single row
with two boolean columns in this order:

- `table_gone` — true when `to_regclass('public.fee_schedule')` is null
- `column_gone` — true when no row in `information_schema.columns` has
  `table_name = 'accounts'` and `column_name = 'fee_tier'`

Both must come back true. The gate also re-reads the catalog itself to
confirm the schema is byte-for-byte what `setup.sql` left.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Nothing in this exercise is a trick. The interesting question is which of
the five statements you expect to survive the rollback — and the answer is
none of them, including the two `ALTER TABLE`s.

## Hint 2
`to_regclass` is the polite way to ask whether a relation exists: it
returns `NULL` instead of raising when the name is unknown.

```sql
SELECT to_regclass('public.nope') IS NULL AS gone;
```

## Hint 3
The final `SELECT` needs no `FROM`. Build the second column as `NOT EXISTS
(SELECT 1 FROM information_schema.columns WHERE table_name = 'accounts'
AND column_name = 'fee_tier')` and alias both columns exactly as the
prompt names them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Try the same migration in your head against a database without
transactional DDL. Where would it stop, and what would you have to write
by hand to get back? That gap is the value of this exercise.

## Hint 2
Two statements would break this if you added them, and knowing which is
the real takeaway: `CREATE INDEX CONCURRENTLY` and `VACUUM` both refuse to
run inside a transaction block with `25001`. A migration that needs a
concurrent index therefore cannot be all-or-nothing, and must be written
to be re-runnable instead.

## Hint 3
Order the file as: `BEGIN;` … five statements … `ROLLBACK;` … then the
verification `SELECT`. The verification must be outside the transaction —
inside it, before the rollback, both answers would be false.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — what an exception handler costs

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Ex3 leaned on a PL/pgSQL exception handler
without saying what it allocates. Prove it.

Write a single `DO $$ ... $$;` block that:

1. writes one row to `ledger` (`account_id` 1, `delta` 0.00, note
   `'probe outer'`), then records `pg_current_xact_id()::text` in a
   variable;
2. opens a nested `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN NULL; END` block
   that writes a second `ledger` row (note `'probe inner'`) and records
   `pg_current_xact_id()::text` again;
3. after the nested block, inserts both readings into `xid_probe (step,
   xid)` as rows `('outer', ...)` and `('inner', ...)`.

The whole `DO` block is one statement, so it is one top-level
transaction — and yet the two readings differ, because the first write
inside the nested block allocated a **subtransaction id**. The gate checks
that `inner` is exactly one greater than `outer`, and that both `ledger`
rows are present (the handler never fires).

That difference is the cost. A backend caches 64 subtransaction ids; past
that its entry overflows and every *other* backend doing a visibility
check on your rows may have to read `pg_subtrans` from disk. This is why
"put an exception handler in the loop" is not free advice.

`pg_current_xact_id()` is PostgreSQL 13+; on older servers the spelling is
`txid_current()`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
An id is only allocated when a transaction — or subtransaction — first
*writes*. Put the `INSERT` before the reading in both places, or you will
measure the wrong moment.

## Hint 2
The nested block is the same construct as ex3, minus the loop:

```sql
BEGIN
  ...            -- runs in a subtransaction
EXCEPTION WHEN OTHERS THEN
  NULL;
END;
```

An exception branch is what turns a plain `BEGIN ... END` grouping into a
subtransaction; without a handler, PL/pgSQL allocates nothing.

## Hint 3
Declare `outer_xid text` and `inner_xid text`. Cast with `::text` because
`pg_current_xact_id()` returns `xid8`, which the gate compares
numerically. The final `INSERT INTO xid_probe (step, xid) VALUES
('outer', outer_xid), ('inner', inner_xid);` goes *after* the nested block
closes.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict first: does the outer reading change after the nested block ends?
It does not — the subtransaction's id is discarded, and the top-level
transaction keeps the id it already had. That asymmetry is why
`pg_subtrans` has to exist at all.

## Hint 2
A useful variation to try by hand afterwards, outside the gate:

```sql
BEGIN;
SELECT pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned();   -- NULL: nothing written yet
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (1, 0, 'x');
SELECT pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned();   -- now it has a value
ROLLBACK;
```

Read-only transactions never burn an id, which is why an idle read replica
does not advance the counter.

## Hint 3
Structure: `DO $$ DECLARE outer_xid text; inner_xid text; BEGIN ... END
$$;`. Everything is straight-line — no loop, no `FOR`. The only subtlety
is remembering that the second `INSERT` has to be inside the nested block,
because that is what forces the subtransaction to become real.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — atomicity without typing BEGIN

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Everything so far used an explicit transaction.
This one must not: your file contains **exactly one statement**, with no
`BEGIN`, `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` anywhere.

Write a single data-modifying-CTE statement that attempts to move
**1000.00 from Alice (id 1) to Bob (id 2)** and write both `ledger` rows
on the way:

```sql
WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE accounts SET balance = balance - 1000.00 WHERE id = 1
  RETURNING id
), logged AS (
  INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note)
  SELECT ... FROM debit
  RETURNING id
)
UPDATE accounts SET ... WHERE id = 2 AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM logged);
```

Alice has 900.00, so the debit violates `CHECK (balance >= 0)` and the
statement raises `23514`. The gate expects that error — and then checks
that **nothing** changed: Alice 900.00, Bob 100.00, `ledger` empty.

No `BEGIN` was typed and no rollback was issued, yet three writes across
two tables were discarded together. Every statement runs inside an
implicit transaction, which is why wrapping a single statement in
`BEGIN`/`COMMIT` buys you nothing but a round trip.

Note that the guard from ex1 is deliberately absent here. With `AND
balance >= 1000.00` the statement would succeed at doing nothing; the
point of this exercise is the failure path.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The failure is the expected outcome. Do not defend against it — the gate
is asserting the error code and the unchanged state, not a successful
transfer.

## Hint 2
All the sub-statements of a data-modifying CTE run in the same snapshot
and the same implicit transaction. That is also why they cannot see each
other's row changes:

```sql
WITH d AS (UPDATE t SET n = n - 1 RETURNING n)
SELECT * FROM t;   -- shows the OLD values
```

You reference `debit` and `logged` through `RETURNING`, never by
re-reading the table.

## Hint 3
The final `UPDATE` is the statement's main body and the two CTEs hang off
it. Chain them so the ledger insert draws from `debit` and the credit is
gated on `logged`; that also documents the intended order for a reader,
even though execution order among CTEs is not otherwise guaranteed.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Count the writes that have to disappear: one `UPDATE`, one `INSERT`, and
one more `UPDATE` that may or may not have run. If any single one of them
survived, the invariant "total balance is 1000.00" would be broken and the
gate would catch it.

## Hint 2
Contrast with a driver-side loop that issues the same three statements
separately in autocommit mode:

```
UPDATE accounts ... id = 1;   -- ERROR 23514, nothing else runs
```

Here the first statement fails on its own and the rest never execute — the
same end state, by luck rather than by guarantee. Change the order so the
credit goes first and autocommit leaves Bob 1000.00 richer.

## Hint 3
`23514` is `check_violation`. If you see `23503` you referenced an account
that does not exist; if you see no error at all, you left a guard in the
`WHERE` clause or picked an amount Alice can afford.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3d01_transaction_atomicity / ex8 — one statement, three writes, all or nothing
-- Expected to fail with SQLSTATE 23514 (check_violation) and leave the
-- database exactly as it was. No BEGIN, no COMMIT, no ROLLBACK.
WITH debit AS (
  UPDATE accounts
     SET balance = balance - 1000.00
   WHERE id = 1
  RETURNING id
), logged AS (
  INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note)
  SELECT id, -1000.00, 'oversized transfer' FROM debit
  RETURNING id
)
UPDATE accounts
   SET balance = balance + 1000.00
 WHERE id = 2
   AND EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM logged);

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a restartable importer

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Combine ex1's guard, ex3's savepoints and
ex8's atomicity into the thing you would actually deploy: an importer that
is safe to run **twice**.

The gate runs your script, records the state, runs it a **second time**,
and requires the state to be identical after both runs. Real importers get
run twice — a retried job, a nervous operator, a queue that delivered the
same message again — and "it corrupted the ledger the second time" is not
an acceptable answer.

Requirements:

- Process `import_rows` in `id` order.
- **Skip** any record whose ledger row already exists. Use the note
  `'import ' || id` as the idempotency key and check for it before doing
  any work.
- Apply `delta` to the named account. A missing account, or a delta that
  would drive the balance negative, is a reject: record it in
  `import_rejects (row_id, sqlstate, message)` and continue with the next
  record. Rejects must also be idempotent — a second run must not insert a
  duplicate reject row.
- On success write the `ledger` row with note `'import ' || id`.
- End the block with `RAISE NOTICE 'applied %, rejected %, skipped %'`.

State after run 1 **and** after run 2: Alice 850.00, Bob 140.00, Escrow
10.00, exactly three `ledger` rows, exactly two `import_rejects` rows.
Run 2 must report three skipped and zero applied.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity challenge`

## Hint 1
Idempotency is not a property of a statement, it is a property you design
in. Ask, per record: "what durable evidence proves this record was already
handled?" You have two kinds of evidence to look for, because a record can
have been applied *or* rejected.

## Hint 2
A cheap existence check inside the loop:

```sql
IF EXISTS (SELECT 1 FROM ledger WHERE note = 'import ' || r.id) THEN
  skipped := skipped + 1;
  CONTINUE;
END IF;
```

`CONTINUE` in PL/pgSQL skips to the next iteration of the enclosing loop.

## Hint 3
Two guards, not one: skip when the ledger row exists, and skip when an
`import_rejects` row exists — otherwise run 2 re-attempts row 2, fails
again, and tries to insert a duplicate `row_id` into a table whose primary
key forbids it, turning your idempotent importer into a crashing one. Keep
the per-record `BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END` from ex3 around the work
only, so the guards are evaluated outside the subtransaction.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Write the second run's behaviour down before you write any code: for each
of the five records, is it applied, rejected, or skipped on run 1, and on
run 2? Rows 2 and 4 are the interesting ones.

## Hint 2
There is a tempting shortcut — make the ledger note unique and let
`ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` swallow the duplicate:

```sql
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (...)
ON CONFLICT (note) DO NOTHING;
```

It does not save you here, because the `UPDATE accounts` has already
happened by then and would be applied a second time. Sector D6 is entirely
about where that shortcut does and does not hold; the ordering rule is
that the idempotency check has to come *before* the side effect.

## Hint 3
Skeleton: declare `r record` and three counters; loop over `import_rows`
ordered by `id`; `CONTINUE` on either guard; inside a nested block do the
`UPDATE`, the `IF NOT FOUND THEN RAISE`, and the `INSERT INTO ledger`;
in the handler insert the reject. The `DO` block is a single statement, so
the entire second run is atomic too — if anything unexpected raises out of
the loop, run 2 leaves no trace.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — commit only if the invariant still holds

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. A different angle on the same idea: a
transaction is a place to *try things and then decide*.

Treasury is sweeping Alice's entire balance into Escrow. Write a single
`DO $$ ... $$;` block that:

1. reads `sum(balance)` across all accounts into `before_total`;
2. reads Alice's current balance into `amt`;
3. debits Alice by `amt` and credits Escrow (id 3) by `amt`;
4. writes two `ledger` rows, note `'sweep'`, deltas `-amt` and `+amt`;
5. re-reads `sum(balance)` into `after_total`;
6. **raises** if `after_total <> before_total`.

Step 6 is the point. Inside a transaction your own writes are visible to
you and to nobody else, so you can inspect the result of your work and
still refuse it. Because the `DO` block is one statement, raising there
discards every write in steps 3 and 4 — you do not compensate, you simply
decline to exist.

Expected final state: Alice 0.00, Escrow 900.00, Bob 100.00, exactly two
`ledger` rows with note `'sweep'`.

To convince yourself the guard works, temporarily change step 3 to credit
`amt + 1` and re-run: the block raises, and the gate's state check shows
nothing moved. Change it back before submitting.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d01_transaction_atomicity review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The invariant is "money is conserved". It is checkable in one line of SQL,
which is exactly why it belongs in the transaction rather than in a
nightly reconciliation report that finds the breach a day later.

## Hint 2
`SELECT ... INTO var` is PL/pgSQL's assignment-from-query form:

```sql
SELECT sum(balance) INTO before_total FROM accounts;
```

Read it *before* the updates, not after — after, both readings would agree
by construction and the check would prove nothing.

## Hint 3
`RAISE EXCEPTION 'invariant broken: % -> %', before_total, after_total;`
gives you a message with the numbers in it. Capture Alice's balance in
`amt` before the debit; using `balance = 0` for the debit and a separately
re-read balance for the credit is the bug this exercise is shaped to
expose.

## Hint 1
Ask which reads inside the block see the updates. All of them — a
statement in PL/pgSQL sees the effects of every earlier statement in the
same transaction. That is what makes step 5 meaningful and what makes the
"check then commit" habit possible at all.

## Hint 2
The same shape without PL/pgSQL, for comparison, is a client that does:

```sql
BEGIN;
UPDATE ...; UPDATE ...; INSERT ...;
SELECT sum(balance) FROM accounts;   -- inspect
COMMIT;    -- or ROLLBACK, decided in application code
```

The `DO` block just moves the decision into the database so no round trip
can be interrupted between inspection and decision.

## Hint 3
Declare three `numeric` variables. Sweep with `UPDATE accounts SET balance
= balance - amt WHERE id = 1` and `... + amt WHERE id = 3`; a
`numeric(12,2)` column and a `numeric` variable compare exactly, so `<>`
is a safe test here in a way it would not be for `double precision`.

lessons.summary: Sector 44 said UPDATE does not update. lessons.briefing:
# V3·D2 — MVCC and what a snapshot actually is

Sector 44 gave you the headline: `UPDATE` writes a new row version and
leaves the old one in place, `DELETE` marks rather than removes, and
`VACUUM` cleans up afterwards. That is enough to explain bloat. It is not
enough to explain why your `SELECT` returned different answers twice in a
row, why a transaction that has been open for six hours makes the whole
cluster slow, or why a row you can plainly see is invisible to the session
next to you.

For that you need the actual mechanism, which is smaller than people
expect: every row version carries two transaction ids, and every query
carries a snapshot. Visibility is a comparison between them.

## The row header

Every tuple in a PostgreSQL table has hidden system columns you can select
by name:

```sql
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, id, qty FROM widget WHERE id = 1;
```

- **`xmin`** — the transaction that created this version.
- **`xmax`** — the transaction that deleted it, *or* the transaction
  currently holding a row lock on it. Zero means neither. That overloading
  matters and sector D4 depends on it.
- **`ctid`** — the physical address, `(page, offset)`. It changes whenever
  a new version is written, which is why it is useless as a permanent
  identifier and excellent as a demonstration.
- `cmin` / `cmax` — command ids, which order statements *within* one
  transaction.

## The snapshot

A snapshot is three things:

```sql
SELECT pg_current_snapshot();   -- e.g. 1234:1240:1236,1238
```

`xmin:xmax:xip_list` reads as: every transaction below `xmin` has
finished, so decide by its commit status alone; every transaction at or
above `xmax` had not started when this snapshot was taken, so it is
invisible; and the explicit list in between names the transactions that
were *in progress* at that instant, which are invisible even if they have
committed since.

A row version is visible to you when its `xmin` is a committed
transaction that your snapshot considers past, and its `xmax` is either
zero, aborted, or a transaction your snapshot considers future. That is
the entire rule. Everything else in this volume — isolation levels, write
skew, `SKIP LOCKED`, vacuum starvation — is a consequence of *when* the
snapshot is taken and *how long* it is held.

`READ COMMITTED`, the default, takes a fresh snapshot at the start of
every statement. `REPEATABLE READ` and `SERIALIZABLE` take one snapshot
at the first statement of the transaction — **not** at `BEGIN` — and keep
it. The review mission is built entirely on that distinction.

## Transaction ids are allocated lazily

A transaction gets a real id only when it first writes. Until then it has
a *virtual* id and burns nothing:

```sql
SELECT pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned();   -- NULL in a read-only txn
SELECT pg_current_xact_id();               -- forces one to be assigned
```

This is why an idle read replica does not advance the counter, why
read-only reporting transactions are cheaper than they look, and why the
`if_assigned` variant is the one you want in a monitoring query — the
other one has a side effect.

## Two sessions, one script

Several missions here need two concurrent connections. The gate reads a
simple interleaving format; you will use it for the rest of this volume.

```sql
-- @A
BEGIN;
SELECT count(*) FROM widget;

-- @B
INSERT INTO widget (id, name, qty) VALUES (6, 'six', 60);

-- @A
SELECT count(*) FROM widget;
COMMIT;
```

The rules:

- A line of exactly `-- @A` or `-- @B` starts a block. Everything up to
  the next marker runs on that session.
- Blocks run **in file order**, and each finishes before the next begins.
  Session state — an open transaction, a `SET`, a held lock — persists
  across that session's blocks.
- Both sessions are autocommit connections, so `BEGIN` and `COMMIT` are
  yours to write.
- Both have `lock_timeout = '5s'`, so a block that blocks forever fails
  the mission instead of hanging the gate. Later sectors add two more
  markers — an expected-error annotation, and `-- @A async` for the cases
  where you genuinely need two blocks running at once.

Order your blocks so that no block waits on a lock held by a later
block — with one exception you will meet in D4, where waiting is the
point and `NOWAIT` makes it fail fast.

## The tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE widget (
  id   int PRIMARY KEY,
  name text NOT NULL,
  qty  int  NOT NULL
);
-- ids 1..5, qty 10, 20, 30, 40, 50

CREATE TABLE horizon_rows (id int PRIMARY KEY, pad text NOT NULL);
-- 5,000 rows; autovacuum is disabled on this table

CREATE TABLE observation (label text PRIMARY KEY, value text NOT NULL);
```

`observation` is how the gates read your answers: missions ask you to
record specific labels, and the gate compares the values. Recording a
reading into a table rather than returning it means the gate can check
what a session saw *at a particular moment in the interleaving*, which is
the only way to grade a concurrency exercise.

## What the eight missions cover

You will watch `ctid` and `xmin` change under an `UPDATE`; prove that a
read-only transaction burns no id; show that uncommitted work is invisible
and committed work becomes visible mid-transaction under `READ
COMMITTED`; show that it does not under `REPEATABLE READ`; read a raw
snapshot and test a specific transaction against it with
`pg_visible_in_snapshot`; discover that a data-modifying CTE cannot see
its own writes; hold the xmin horizon open with one session and watch
`VACUUM` fail to reclaim anything; and catch `xmax` in its second job, as
a row lock. The challenge builds a visibility report over a table you have
half-modified. The review pins down exactly when a repeatable-read
snapshot is taken.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3d02_mvcc_snapshots

The useful reframing: PostgreSQL does not have "the current state of the
table". It has a pile of row versions and a rule for deciding which ones
you are allowed to look at. "The current state" is a per-observer
computation, and once you believe that, most concurrency surprises stop
being surprises.

## Notes

**Visibility is decided per row version, not per row.** There is no lock
taken, no coordination, and no communication with the writing session. A
reader looks at `xmin`, consults the commit status, compares against its
snapshot, and decides alone. This is why readers never block writers and
writers never block readers in PostgreSQL, and it is the single largest
architectural difference from a lock-based system like SQL Server's
default isolation.

**`xmax` is overloaded and this trips people up.** A non-zero `xmax` may
mean "deleted by transaction N" or "row-locked by transaction N" or, for
multiple shared lockers, "see multixact N" — the `infomask` bits
distinguish them, and they are not exposed as a nice column. Never write
application logic that reads `xmax`. Read it to learn, as in ex8.

**Snapshot timing is the whole of isolation.** `READ COMMITTED` refreshing
per statement is why the same query twice in one transaction can differ.
`REPEATABLE READ` holding one snapshot is why it cannot. Neither is more
"correct"; they answer different questions, and D3 is about choosing.

**The snapshot's `xmin` is the horizon, and it is a cluster-wide cost.**
While your transaction holds a snapshot, no row version that was live at
that moment may be removed by `VACUUM` — in *any* table, not just the ones
you touched. One forgotten `BEGIN` in a psql window can therefore bloat a
database that session never queried. Ex7 makes that concrete; D8 makes it
operational.

**A statement sees its own transaction's earlier statements but not its
own effects.** Command ids give the ordering. This is what stops an
`UPDATE widget SET qty = qty + 1` from finding the rows it just wrote and
incrementing them forever — the Halloween problem, named after the day it
was discovered in 1976 — and it is why a data-modifying CTE reads the
table as it was before the statement began.

**Hint bits make the second read cheaper.** The first reader to resolve a
tuple's commit status writes the answer back into the tuple header as a
hint bit. That is a *write*, which is why a plain `SELECT` over a
freshly-loaded table can dirty pages and generate I/O, and why the second
run of the same query is often mysteriously faster and quieter.

## ex1 — the row moves

`ctid` before and after tell you the update wrote a new tuple; `xmin`
before and after tell you which transaction wrote it. Worth noticing that
the old version is still on disk at the old `ctid` — invisible to you, and
still needed by any older snapshot.

## ex2 — nothing was spent

A transaction that only reads never appears in anyone's `xip` list,
because it never has an id to appear as. Use
`pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`; the plain form would assign one and
destroy the thing you are measuring.

## ex3 — uncommitted, then committed

Two readings, one interleaving. The first proves dirty reads are
impossible in PostgreSQL at any isolation level. The second proves that
`READ COMMITTED` will happily change its mind inside a single transaction,
which is the anomaly D3 calls a non-repeatable read.

## ex4 — the same interleaving, one word different

`BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ` and the second reading stops
changing. Note carefully that A must *read* before B commits: the snapshot
is taken at the first statement, and if A's first statement comes after
B's commit there is nothing to be repeatable about.

## ex5 — reading the snapshot itself

`pg_current_snapshot()` and `pg_visible_in_snapshot(xid8, snapshot)` turn
the rule from prose into something you can assert on. B's id sits in A's
`xip` list while B is open; after B commits and A takes a *new* snapshot,
the same id is visible. The old snapshot, if you kept it in a variable,
still says invisible — a snapshot is a value, not a subscription.

## ex6 — the CTE cannot see itself

```sql
WITH bumped AS (UPDATE widget SET qty = qty + 100 RETURNING id)
SELECT count(*) FROM widget WHERE qty >= 100;
```

Zero. Both halves of the statement read the same snapshot, taken before
the statement started. This is the single most common surprise with
data-modifying CTEs, and the reason you thread results through `RETURNING`
rather than re-reading the table.

## ex7 — the horizon

One `REPEATABLE READ` reader, 5,000 deleted rows, and a `VACUUM` that
reclaims none of them. Then the reader commits, the same `VACUUM` reclaims
all of them, and nothing else changed. If you ever need to explain to a
product manager why a long-running report is a database problem, this is
the two-minute demonstration.

## ex8 — xmax as a lock

`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` writes your transaction id into the row's `xmax`
without deleting anything. Row locks in PostgreSQL live in the tuple, not
in a lock table, which is why you can lock ten million rows without
exhausting `max_locks_per_transaction` — and why taking a row lock dirties
the page and generates WAL.

## Further reading

- [Transaction Isolation](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/transaction-iso.html) — the visibility rules stated normatively.
- [System Columns](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/ddl-system-columns.html) — `ctid`, `xmin`, `xmax`, `cmin`, `cmax`.
- [Transaction ID and Snapshot Information Functions](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-info.html#FUNCTIONS-PG-SNAPSHOT) — `pg_current_snapshot`, `pg_visible_in_snapshot`, `pg_snapshot_xmin`.
- [Routine Vacuuming](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/routine-vacuuming.html) — the horizon, freezing, and wraparound.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·D2 — MVCC and what a snapshot actually is (archive)

## Concepts

### The visibility test, in full

For a row version with `xmin = X` and `xmax = Y`, seen through a snapshot
`S = (S.xmin, S.xmax, S.xip)`:

1. If `X` is my own transaction and its command id is earlier than the
   current statement's — visible (subject to `Y`).
2. If `X >= S.xmax`, or `X ∈ S.xip` — the creator had not committed when
   the snapshot was taken. **Invisible.**
3. If `X < S.xmin` or `X` is otherwise past, look up `X` in `pg_xact`. If
   it aborted — **invisible**. If it committed, continue.
4. If `Y` is zero — **visible**.
5. If `Y` is a lock rather than a delete (an `infomask` bit says so) —
   **visible**.
6. If `Y >= S.xmax`, or `Y ∈ S.xip`, or `Y` aborted — the deleter is not
   past for me. **Visible.**
7. Otherwise the deleter committed in my past. **Invisible.**

Every isolation-level behaviour in the next sector follows from step 2 and
step 6 plus the question of when `S` was taken.

### Inspecting it

```sql
SELECT ctid, xmin, xmax, cmin, cmax, * FROM widget ORDER BY id;

SELECT pg_current_snapshot()                     AS snap,
       pg_snapshot_xmin(pg_current_snapshot())   AS horizon,
       pg_snapshot_xmax(pg_current_snapshot())   AS next_unassigned,
       pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()          AS my_xid;

SELECT * FROM pg_snapshot_xip(pg_current_snapshot());   -- in-progress ids
```

`age(xmin)` gives the number of transactions since a version was created,
which is the number that matters for freezing and wraparound:

```sql
SELECT id, age(xmin) AS versions_old FROM widget ORDER BY 2 DESC LIMIT 5;
```

### Worked example: the two readings

```sql
-- @A
BEGIN;                                   -- READ COMMITTED (default)
SELECT count(*) FROM widget;             -- 5

-- @B
INSERT INTO widget (id, name, qty) VALUES (6, 'six', 60);   -- autocommit

-- @A
SELECT count(*) FROM widget;             -- 6  <- new snapshot this statement
COMMIT;
```

Change A's first line to `BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;` and the
second count is 5. Nothing else changes. That one-line diff is the whole
of the next sector in miniature.

### Worked example: the horizon

```sql
-- @B
BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
SELECT count(*) FROM horizon_rows;       -- takes the snapshot

-- @A
DELETE FROM horizon_rows;
VACUUM (ANALYZE) horizon_rows;
SELECT n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'horizon_rows';
-- 5000: B might still need those versions

-- @B
COMMIT;

-- @A
VACUUM (ANALYZE) horizon_rows;
SELECT n_dead_tup FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'horizon_rows';
-- 0
```

B never touched a row. B's *snapshot* is what pinned them.

### When xmax is not a transaction id

A single `xmax` field has to represent "everyone currently holding this
row", and more than one transaction can hold a row in a shared mode at
once. When that happens PostgreSQL allocates a **multixact id** and puts
that in `xmax` instead, with an `infomask` bit saying so. The membership
list lives in `pg_multixact`, a pair of SLRUs with the same shape — and
the same failure modes — as `pg_subtrans`.

Two practical consequences. Multixact ids are 32 bits and wrap, so they
have their own freezing machinery and their own
`autovacuum_multixact_freeze_max_age`; a workload that takes many shared
row locks (heavy foreign-key traffic on a hot parent row is the classic)
can trigger anti-wraparound vacuums on multixacts specifically, which
surprises people who only ever look at `age(datfrozenxid)`. And
`SELECT ... FOR SHARE` on the same row from many sessions is a genuine
scalability cliff rather than the free operation it looks like.

```sql
SELECT * FROM pg_stat_user_tables WHERE relname = 'widget';
SELECT datname, mxid_age(datminmxid) FROM pg_database;
```

### Worked example: a statement cannot see itself

```sql
BEGIN;
INSERT INTO widget (id, name, qty) VALUES (8, 'eight', 80);
SELECT count(*) FROM widget;                      -- 6: an earlier statement

WITH bumped AS (UPDATE widget SET qty = qty + 100 RETURNING id),
     tally  AS (SELECT count(*) AS c FROM bumped),
     seen   AS (SELECT count(*) AS c FROM widget WHERE qty >= 100)
SELECT (SELECT c FROM seen) AS visible_now,       -- 0
       (SELECT c FROM tally) AS actually_updated; -- 6
COMMIT;

SELECT count(*) FROM widget WHERE qty >= 100;     -- 6
```

The update happened, and the statement that performed it could not see the
result. Between statements, permissive; within one, never.

## Common mistakes

1. **Treating `ctid` as an identifier.** It changes on every update and is
   reused after vacuum. Useful for `WHERE ctid = ...` in a
   delete-duplicates one-liner within a single statement, never for
   storage.
2. **Calling `pg_current_xact_id()` in a monitoring query.** It assigns an
   id, advancing the counter and turning a read-only session into a
   writer. Use `pg_current_xact_id_if_assigned()`.
3. **Reading `xmax` to decide whether a row is deleted.** A non-zero
   `xmax` may be a lock, an aborted delete, or a multixact.
4. **Expecting a data-modifying CTE to see its own writes.** It cannot;
   thread the values through `RETURNING`.
5. **Believing `REPEATABLE READ` takes its snapshot at `BEGIN`.** It takes
   it at the first statement. `BEGIN; <two seconds of application logic>;
   SELECT ...` is not the transaction you think it is.
6. **Assuming a read-only transaction is free.** It is free of transaction
   ids and of WAL, but not of the horizon: its snapshot still stops
   `VACUUM` cluster-wide.
7. **Blaming `SELECT` for I/O it did not cause.** Hint bit writes and
   opportunistic page pruning mean a read query can dirty pages. This is
   normal and it settles.
8. **Assuming other databases work this way.** Oracle keeps an undo log
   and reconstructs old versions on demand; MySQL/InnoDB does the same and
   stores current data in place. Only PostgreSQL leaves the old versions
   in the heap, which is exactly why it needs `VACUUM` and they do not.

## The interview answer

> *"Explain MVCC in PostgreSQL."*

Each row version carries the id of the transaction that created it
(`xmin`) and the id of the one that deleted or locked it (`xmax`). Each
query carries a snapshot: the lowest still-running transaction id, the
