Phase 1 models an application that reads a value, computes a new one, and
writes it back. `observation` stands in for the application's variables.

```
-- @A  BEGIN;  record 'a_read' = counter 'hits'.n              (0)
-- @B  BEGIN;  record 'b_read' = counter 'hits'.n              (0)
-- @A  UPDATE counter SET n = (SELECT value::int FROM observation
--                             WHERE label = 'a_read') + 1
--       WHERE name = 'hits';
--      COMMIT;
-- @B  the same update, reading 'b_read';  COMMIT;
-- @A  record 'lost_update_final' = counter 'hits'.n           (expect 1)
```

Two transactions each added one to a counter that started at zero, and it
ends at one. B's write was computed from a value that stopped being true
before B wrote it, and nothing warned anybody.

Phase 2 does the arithmetic in the database:

```
-- @A  UPDATE counter SET n = 0 WHERE name = 'hits';     -- reset
-- @A  BEGIN; UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits'; COMMIT;
-- @B  BEGIN; UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits'; COMMIT;
-- @A  record 'atomic_final' = counter 'hits'.n          (expect 2)
```

`n = n + 1` cannot lose an increment at any isolation level, because the
expression is evaluated by the server against the current row version
*after* the row lock is granted. This is the single most valuable rule in
this sector: **if a read-modify-write can be written as one statement,
write it as one statement**, and no isolation reasoning is required.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The bug in phase 1 is not the isolation level. It is that the new value
was computed somewhere the database could not see, from data that had
already expired by the time the write arrived.

## Hint 2
Reading a stored "application variable" back inside a statement:

```sql
UPDATE counter
   SET n = (SELECT value::int FROM observation WHERE label = 'a_read') + 1
 WHERE name = 'hits';
```

The subquery sees A's own uncommitted `observation` row, because a
transaction always sees its own earlier statements.

## Hint 3
Nine blocks. B's update in phase 1 does not block, because A has already
committed by then — the lost update needs no lock contention at all, which
is why it is so easy to ship.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what a lock would have done. `SELECT n FROM counter WHERE name =
'hits' FOR UPDATE` in both A and B would serialise them, and B's read
would return 1 rather than 0. That is the third fix, and D4 is about when
it is the right one.

## Hint 2
The same class of bug in the wild rarely looks like a counter:

```sql
SELECT settings FROM account WHERE id = 7;      -- a JSON blob
-- application merges one key
UPDATE account SET settings = $1 WHERE id = 7;  -- writes the whole blob
```

Two concurrent preference changes, one survives. The fix is the same
shape: `SET settings = settings || $1` does the merge server-side.

## Hint 3
Phase 2's reset must be its own statement outside a transaction, and it
must come after `lost_update_final` is recorded — otherwise you overwrite
the evidence before reading it.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — 40001, and why the retry needs a new transaction

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run ex4's phase-1 schedule at `REPEATABLE READ`
and watch the level refuse rather than lose.

```
-- @A  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     SELECT n FROM counter WHERE name = 'hits';   -- takes the snapshot
-- @B  UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';   -- autocommit
-- @A expect 40001
--     UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';
-- @A  record 'after_failure_n' = counter 'hits'.n         (expect 1)
-- @A  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';
--     COMMIT;
-- @A  record 'after_retry_n'   = counter 'hits'.n         (expect 2)
```

The `-- @A expect 40001` marker tells the gate that block must raise
`could not serialize access due to concurrent update`, and that it should
roll session A back afterwards. A block with an `expect` that succeeds
fails the mission.

The message is precise: A's snapshot predates B's commit, so applying A's
update would mean writing on top of a version A cannot see. `REPEATABLE
READ` will not silently use the new version (that would be a
non-repeatable read) and will not silently overwrite it (that would be a
lost update), so it aborts.

Note what does **not** work: retrying the same statement in the same
transaction. The snapshot is a property of the transaction; only ending it
gets you a new one. The last two blocks are the correct shape, and ex8
shows the incorrect one failing on purpose.

Nothing you record before the failing block survives — the abort discards
it — which is why every reading here happens after A has been rolled
back.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A's first `SELECT` looks decorative. It is the statement that takes the
snapshot, and without it A's snapshot would be taken *after* B's commit
and the update would succeed — no error, no lesson.

## Hint 2
The marker goes on the block line, with the SQLSTATE:

```
-- @A expect 40001
UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';
```

`40001` is `serialization_failure`. Its sibling `40P01` is
`deadlock_detected`, and a retry loop should treat them identically.

## Hint 3
Six blocks, all on session A except one. Do not put `COMMIT` in the
`expect` block: the transaction is already doomed, and the gate handles
the rollback.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Compare the outcome with ex4 phase 1 honestly. There, two increments
produced 1 and nobody knew. Here, two increments produce 2 — but only
because you wrote a retry. `REPEATABLE READ` did not fix the bug; it made
the bug your problem at a moment when you can still act.

## Hint 2
The same failure appears in ORMs as an unhandled exception at a random
call site, because the level was set globally and the retry was never
written:

```
psycopg.errors.SerializationFailure: could not serialize access due to
concurrent update
```

If you raise the level anywhere, own the retry everywhere.

## Hint 3
`after_failure_n` should be 1, not 0 — B's increment committed and stands.
If you get 0, B's block is in the wrong place; if you get 2, A's failing
update somehow succeeded and the `expect` marker will already have failed
the mission for you.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Say precisely what each transaction read and what it wrote. A read
{alice, bob}, wrote {alice}. B read {alice, bob}, wrote {bob}. The write
sets are disjoint — that is exactly why snapshot isolation cannot see the
problem.

## Hint 2
The predicate locks that make phase 2 work are visible while it runs:

```sql
SELECT locktype, relation::regclass, mode
  FROM pg_locks WHERE mode = 'SIReadLock';
```

They block nothing. They exist only so the conflict detector can find the
read/write edges.

## Hint 3
Ten blocks. Both phase-1 counts must be taken before either update, or A's
commit lands inside B's snapshot and B decides not to leave. The reset in
phase 2 is a bare autocommit `UPDATE` on session A, outside any
transaction.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Try to fix phase 1 without changing the level, and notice what fails.
Adding `FOR UPDATE` to the count query is the standard reflex — and it
works here, because it locks the rows both transactions read. That is the
challenge, and the reason it works is worth understanding before you write
it.

## Hint 2
Write skew is the anomaly behind a long list of real incidents: two
refunds against one balance, two bookings for one seat, two people
promoted into a role limited to one. The tell is always the same shape —

```
read a set  ->  decide  ->  write a row that was not in what you read
```

Search your codebase for that shape rather than for a keyword.

## Hint 3
If phase 2's B block succeeds instead of failing, check that both
transactions really are `SERIALIZABLE` — SSI reasons only about
serializable transactions, and one `REPEATABLE READ` participant makes the
whole analysis blind.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — EvalPlanQual: the re-check nobody teaches

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. This mission needs a block that genuinely waits,
so it uses the `async` marker: `-- @B async` starts the block without
waiting for it, and `-- @join` waits for every outstanding async block.

Phase 1 — a conditional update that arrives late.

```
-- @A        BEGIN; UPDATE task SET status = 'claimed' WHERE id = 1;
-- @B async  WITH u AS (
--             UPDATE task SET owner = 'bob'
--              WHERE id = 1 AND status = 'pending' RETURNING id)
--           INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
--           SELECT 'epq_rows', count(*)::text FROM u;
-- @A        COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'epq_owner'  = coalesce(owner, 'NULL') for task 1
--           record 'epq_status' = status for task 1
```

B blocks on A's row lock. When A commits, B does **not** simply apply
itself to whatever is there now: at `READ COMMITTED` it re-runs its own
`WHERE` clause against the new row version. `status` is `'claimed'`, the
predicate fails, and the row is skipped. Expect `epq_rows` = `0`,
`epq_owner` = `NULL`, `epq_status` = `claimed`.

Phase 2 — the same schedule with no predicate.

```
-- @A        BEGIN; UPDATE task SET status = 'claimed' WHERE id = 2;
-- @B async  WITH u AS (UPDATE task SET owner = 'carol'
--                       WHERE id = 2 RETURNING id)
--           INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
--           SELECT 'no_predicate_rows', count(*)::text FROM u;
-- @A        COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'task2_owner'  (expect 'carol')
--           record 'task2_status' (expect 'claimed')
```

One row updated, applied on top of A's version. Both statements "worked";
only one of them checked whether its assumption still held.

The rule to take away: at `READ COMMITTED`, put the assumption in the
`WHERE` clause and check the row count. That is what makes `UPDATE task
SET status='done' WHERE id = $1 AND status='pending'` a safe claim, and it
is the foundation of the queue pattern in D4.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask what the alternatives would be when B unblocks. Apply blindly (lost
update), fail with 40001 (that is `REPEATABLE READ`), or re-check the
predicate. `READ COMMITTED` chose the third, and the choice is invisible
until you look for it.

## Hint 2
Capturing an updated row count without a client:

```sql
WITH u AS (UPDATE t SET ... WHERE ... RETURNING 1)
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'label', count(*)::text FROM u;
```

`RETURNING` feeding a `count(*)` is the SQL-only equivalent of reading the
command tag.

## Hint 3
The `async` block must be the one that waits, and the block that releases
it must come after. If you forget `-- @join`, the readings after it may
run before B has finished and you will see stale values — join before you
observe.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict phase 2 before running. Most people expect the unconditional
update to also be skipped, on the grounds that "the row changed". Nothing
in it asked whether the row changed, so nothing checked.

## Hint 2
EvalPlanQual explains a behaviour you may already have hit and blamed on
something else:

```sql
UPDATE inventory SET stock = stock - 1
 WHERE sku = 'X' AND stock > 0;
```

Under heavy concurrency this never oversells, even at `READ COMMITTED`,
because every waiter re-checks `stock > 0` against the version it finally
sees. Remove the guard and it oversells immediately.

## Hint 3
`coalesce(owner, 'NULL')` is deliberate: `observation.value` is `NOT
NULL`, and an unset owner is the expected answer in phase 1. If your
insert silently writes nothing, that is why.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the retry loop that can never succeed

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. Write the mistake deliberately, and measure it.

A `REPEATABLE READ` transaction hits 40001. You catch it in PL/pgSQL and
retry — three times, in a loop, inside the same transaction. Record each
attempt's outcome, then prove a fresh transaction succeeds immediately.

```
-- @A  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     SELECT n FROM counter WHERE name = 'hits';     -- snapshot
-- @B  UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';   -- autocommit
-- @A  DO block: FOR i IN 1..3, try the UPDATE, catch serialization_failure,
--     record 'attempt_1' / 'attempt_2' / 'attempt_3' as 'succeeded' or '40001'
--     COMMIT;
-- @A  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';
--     COMMIT;
-- @A  record 'final_n' = counter 'hits'.n
```

Expected: all three attempts `40001`, `final_n` = `2`.

Two mechanisms are on display. Catching the error works — the nested
`BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END` is a subtransaction, so the outer
transaction stays usable and A can still commit, which is why the
`attempt_*` observations survive. And retrying is useless — the snapshot
belongs to the transaction, and the transaction has not ended, so attempt
2 compares against exactly the same snapshot as attempt 1.

The structural conclusion: **a retry loop must live outside the
transaction it retries.** In a PL/pgSQL function you cannot write one at
all, because a function runs inside its caller's transaction. This is a
real limitation, not a gap in your knowledge, and the answer is a client
retry or a wrapper procedure that uses `COMMIT` — legal in a `CALL`ed
procedure, illegal in a function.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Before writing it, decide what would have to change between attempt 1 and
attempt 2 for attempt 2 to succeed. Then check whether anything in the
loop changes it.

## Hint 2
The catchable condition has a name:

```sql
EXCEPTION WHEN serialization_failure THEN
  outcome := '40001';
```

`deadlock_detected` is its neighbour. Both are transient by nature, which
is exactly what makes catching them here so tempting and so wrong.

## Hint 3
Structure the `DO` block as `FOR i IN 1..3 LOOP` containing a nested
`BEGIN ... EXCEPTION ... END`, then an `INSERT INTO observation` using
`'attempt_' || i` as the label. Keep the insert outside the nested block
so it is not discarded when the handler fires.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
There is a second, quieter lesson in the fact that A can commit at all
after three failed attempts. A subtransaction absorbed each failure, so
the outer transaction was never poisoned — which means a function full of
exception handlers can commit having silently done nothing. Log your
handlers.

## Hint 2
The shape that does work, for comparison, is a procedure rather than a
function:

```sql
CREATE PROCEDURE bump() LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  LOOP
    BEGIN
      UPDATE counter SET n = n + 1 WHERE name = 'hits';
      COMMIT;              -- legal in a procedure, not in a function
      EXIT;
    EXCEPTION WHEN serialization_failure THEN
      ROLLBACK;
    END;
  END LOOP;
END $$;
```

`CALL bump();` from autocommit. Procedures gained transaction control in
PostgreSQL 11 precisely for this.

## Hint 3
If any attempt records `succeeded`, check that B's update really committed
before the `DO` block and that A's snapshot was taken before B's update —
A's `SELECT` in the first block is what fixes it.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — fixing write skew without SERIALIZABLE

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. `SERIALIZABLE` is not always available:
maybe other services share the database at `READ COMMITTED`, maybe the
abort rate is unacceptable, maybe you cannot retry. Fix the on-call
invariant anyway, at the default level.

The technique is to **materialise the conflict**: take a row lock on
everything the decision depends on, so two deciders cannot decide at once.

Write, in this order:

1. A function

   ```sql
   CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION try_go_off_call(p_name text)
     RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ ... $$;
   ```

   that locks every currently-on-call doctor row with `FOR UPDATE` in a
   deterministic order, counts how many would remain on call if `p_name`
   left, returns `false` without writing if that count is below 1, and
   otherwise sets `on_call = false` for `p_name` and returns `true`.

2. This interleaving, at `READ COMMITTED` throughout:

```
-- @A        BEGIN;
--           record 'a_result' = try_go_off_call('alice')::text
-- @B async  BEGIN;
--           record 'b_result' = try_go_off_call('bob')::text
-- @A        COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @B        COMMIT;
-- @A        record 'left_on_call' = count(*) FROM doctor WHERE on_call
```

Expected: `a_result` = `true`, `b_result` = `false`, `left_on_call` = `1`.

B's call blocks inside the function, on the row lock A holds over `alice`.
When A commits, B's locking select re-checks its predicate against the new
versions (ex7's EvalPlanQual), finds `alice` no longer on call, locks only
`bob`, counts zero remaining, and declines.

Order the lock acquisition — `ORDER BY name` — even though it looks
unnecessary with one caller per doctor. Two sessions locking the same set
in different orders is a deadlock, and D5 is entirely about the habit this
line represents.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The reason `SERIALIZABLE` was needed in ex6 is that the two transactions
read a set and wrote outside it. If reading the set also *locks* it, the
second reader cannot proceed until the first has finished writing — the
conflict becomes a lock conflict, which `READ COMMITTED` handles.

## Hint 2
`PERFORM` is how PL/pgSQL runs a query for its effects, and `FOR UPDATE`
is the effect you want:

```sql
PERFORM 1 FROM doctor WHERE on_call ORDER BY name FOR UPDATE;
```

The rows are locked until the calling transaction ends — not until the
function returns.

## Hint 3
Four statements in the function body: the locking `PERFORM`; a
`SELECT count(*) INTO remaining FROM doctor WHERE on_call AND name <>
p_name`; an `IF remaining < 1 THEN RETURN false; END IF;`; and the
`UPDATE` plus `RETURN true`. Note that the count must exclude `p_name`
itself — it is asking "who is left if I go", not "who is on call".
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask why the lock has to be taken on rows the transaction may never write.
Locking only `alice` would let B lock only `bob` and both would proceed —
the lock has to cover the *read set that the decision depends on*, which
is the same set `SERIALIZABLE` would have predicate-locked for you.

## Hint 2
The alternative technique, worth knowing and often better, is to give the
invariant a home:

```sql
CREATE TABLE roster (id int PRIMARY KEY, on_call_count int NOT NULL
                     CHECK (on_call_count >= 1));
```

Now every leaver decrements one row, the row lock is automatic, and the
`CHECK` enforces the rule for every client at every isolation level,
including the ones written next year by someone who has not read this.
Denormalisation as a correctness tool, not a performance one.

## Hint 3
If `b_result` comes back `true`, B is not blocking — check that the
`PERFORM ... FOR UPDATE` is the first statement in the function body, and
that A has not committed before B's block starts (that is what `async`
is for).

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — the anomaly only predicate locks can catch

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. A different shape from ex6: here the
conflicting writes are **inserts**, so there is no existing row for
anybody to lock, and `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` cannot save you.

`mytab` holds `(class, value)` pairs: class 1 has 10 and 20, class 2 has
100 and 200. Two transactions each sum one class and insert the total into
the *other* class.

Phase 1, `REPEATABLE READ`:

```
-- @A  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     INSERT INTO mytab (class, value)
--     SELECT 2, sum(value)::int FROM mytab WHERE class = 1;     -- 30
-- @B  BEGIN ISOLATION LEVEL REPEATABLE READ;
--     INSERT INTO mytab (class, value)
--     SELECT 1, sum(value)::int FROM mytab WHERE class = 2;     -- 300
-- @A  COMMIT;
-- @B  COMMIT;
-- @A  record 'rr_class1_sum' = sum(value) WHERE class = 1       (expect 330)
--     record 'rr_class2_sum' = sum(value) WHERE class = 2       (expect 330)
```

Both commit. There is no serial order that produces this state: run A
first and B would have summed 130; run B first and A would have summed
330. The result corresponds to no possible sequential execution, and
`REPEATABLE READ` allowed it because neither transaction modified a row
the other read.

Phase 2 — delete the two rows phase 1 added (`DELETE FROM mytab WHERE id >
4`) and run the identical schedule at `SERIALIZABLE`, with B's commit
marked `-- @B expect 40001`. Then record `ssi_row_count` = `count(*)` from
`mytab` (expect 5: the original four plus A's insert).

This is the example in the PostgreSQL manual, and it is the clearest
argument for SSI: the anomaly involves rows that did not exist when the
transactions started, so no row lock could have prevented it. Only a
record of the *predicate* each transaction read — `WHERE class = 1` — can
detect the conflict.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d03_isolation_levels review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Work out both serial orders by hand before running, and write the two
possible legal outcomes as a comment. The observed outcome matches
neither; that is the definition of a serialization anomaly.

## Hint 2
Inserting a computed aggregate:

```sql
INSERT INTO mytab (class, value)
SELECT 2, sum(value)::int FROM mytab WHERE class = 1;
```

`sum` returns `numeric` over `int` input, hence the cast. `id` is a
`serial` and fills itself in.

## Hint 3
Eleven blocks. The reset between phases is a bare `DELETE FROM mytab WHERE
id > 4;` on session A outside a transaction; without it, phase 2's sums
differ and B may fail for a different reason — which would still pass the
`expect` marker while proving the wrong thing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what you would lock to prevent this at `READ COMMITTED`. The rows A
read are not the rows B wrote — B wrote a row that did not exist. The only
lockable object covering "all rows where class = 1" is the table itself,
and `LOCK TABLE mytab IN SHARE ROW EXCLUSIVE MODE` really is the
`READ COMMITTED` fix here. Compare its cost to an occasional 40001.

## Hint 2
The third option, and usually the best one, removes the aggregate from the
critical path entirely: keep a `class_total` row per class, updated in the
same statement that inserts, so the invariant lives on one lockable row.
The recurring theme of this volume is that a well-chosen row is cheaper
than a well-chosen isolation level.

## Hint 3
Phase 2's failure may appear on B's `INSERT` or on B's `COMMIT` depending
on when the conflict is detected; put both inside the `expect` block. If
neither raises, verify both transactions opened with `ISOLATION LEVEL
SERIALIZABLE` — a single non-serializable participant disables the whole
analysis.

lessons.title: V3·D4 — Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and queue tables
lessons.summary: Four row-lock strengths, a compatibility matrix you build yourself, and the two clauses that turn a table into a work queue. Plus the trap that makes a naive claim query return nothing while nine jobs sit waiting, and the dequeue statement that survives twelve workers.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·D4 — Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and queue tables

D3 ended with a fix that was not an isolation level: lock the rows the
decision depends on, and the anomaly becomes a lock conflict the default
level already handles. This sector is about that instrument in detail —
what the four lock strengths are, what they conflict with, how they are
stored, and the one clause, `SKIP LOCKED`, that turns a boring table into
the most reliable job queue most systems will ever need.

## The four strengths

```sql
SELECT ... FOR KEY SHARE;        -- weakest
SELECT ... FOR SHARE;
SELECT ... FOR NO KEY UPDATE;
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;           -- strongest
```

They exist because "locked" is not one thing. A foreign key check needs to
know the parent row's *key* will not change or disappear; it does not care
about the parent's balance. So an `INSERT INTO payment` takes `FOR KEY
SHARE` on the referenced `account` row, and a plain `UPDATE account SET
balance = ...` takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` — and those two are **compatible**,
which is why updating a customer's name no longer blocks inserting their
orders. Before PostgreSQL 9.3 there were only two strengths and it did.

The rule of thumb: use `FOR UPDATE` when you intend to delete the row or
change a key column; `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` when you will update a non-key
column; `FOR SHARE` when you need the row to stay as it is while you read
it; `FOR KEY SHARE` almost never explicitly. Ex7 has you build the
compatibility matrix by experiment rather than reading it.

## Where a row lock lives

Not in a lock table. D2's ex8 showed it: the locking transaction's id goes
into the tuple's `xmax`, with `infomask` bits recording the strength. The
consequences are worth stating plainly.

- You can lock ten million rows without touching
  `max_locks_per_transaction`, because there is no per-row lock entry in
  shared memory.
- Taking a row lock is a **write**: it dirties the page and generates WAL.
  `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a large result set is an I/O-heavy operation
  that looks like a read in your code.
- When two transactions hold the same row in compatible modes, one `xmax`
  cannot name both, so PostgreSQL allocates a **multixact** id and stores
  the membership in `pg_multixact`. Heavy shared locking has its own
  wraparound and its own SLRU contention.

There *is* a transient heavyweight lock involved — a "tuple lock" that
serialises waiters queueing for the same row, visible in `pg_locks` as
`locktype = 'tuple'` — but it is held only while acquiring, not for the
duration.

## Waiting, or not

```sql
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;               -- wait indefinitely
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;        -- 55P03 immediately if held
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;   -- silently omit locked rows
SET lock_timeout = '300ms';          -- wait a bounded time, then 55P03
```

`NOWAIT` and `lock_timeout` produce the same SQLSTATE, `55P03`, with
different messages. `statement_timeout` produces `57014` instead, and
applies to the whole statement rather than to lock acquisition — which is
why a job that must not wait on a lock but may legitimately take thirty
seconds to run needs both settings, not one.

`SKIP LOCKED` is different in kind: it does not fail, it returns fewer
rows. That makes it wrong for anything where the row set matters and
exactly right for a queue, where "give me some work nobody else is doing"
is the actual requirement.

## The queue

```sql
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM job
   WHERE state = 'ready' AND run_after <= now()
   ORDER BY run_after, id
   LIMIT 5
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
)
UPDATE job j
   SET state = 'running', locked_at = now(), locked_by = $1,
       attempts = attempts + 1
  FROM claimed c
 WHERE j.id = c.id
RETURNING j.id, j.payload;
```

Every clause is load-bearing. `ORDER BY` gives fairness; `LIMIT` bounds
the batch; `FOR UPDATE` takes the lock that makes the claim exclusive;
`SKIP LOCKED` sends each worker to different rows instead of a queue
behind one row; the `UPDATE ... RETURNING` makes the claim durable and
hands you the work in one round trip. Twelve workers running this
statement in a loop scale nearly linearly, and it is a great deal less
infrastructure than a message broker.

What it does not give you: at-most-once delivery. A worker that dies after
claiming leaves a row in `running` forever unless something reaps it,
which is what the challenge builds.

## The trap in the middle of the sector

```sql
SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE;
```

Two workers run this. Worker A gets job 1 and updates it; worker B blocks
on the row lock. When A commits, B's lock is granted, EvalPlanQual
re-checks `state = 'ready'` against the new version, the row no longer
matches — and B gets **zero rows**, while nine ready jobs sit untouched.
The `LIMIT` was applied before the locking, so there is no second candidate
to fall back to. Ex8 makes you watch it, and `SKIP LOCKED` is the fix.

## The tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE job (
  id        bigserial PRIMARY KEY,
  state     text        NOT NULL DEFAULT 'ready',
  payload   text        NOT NULL,
  attempts  int         NOT NULL DEFAULT 0,
  run_after timestamptz NOT NULL DEFAULT now(),
  locked_at timestamptz,
  locked_by text
);
-- ids 1..10, all 'ready', run_after now()

CREATE TABLE account (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text NOT NULL,
                      balance numeric(12,2) NOT NULL);
-- 1 alice 100.00, 2 bob 200.00

CREATE TABLE payment (id serial PRIMARY KEY,
                      account_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES account(id),
                      amount numeric(12,2) NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE observation (label text PRIMARY KEY, value text NOT NULL);
```

The interleaving format, the `expect <sqlstate>` annotation and
`async` / `@join` all work exactly as in D2 and D3.

## What the eight missions cover

`NOWAIT` and its SQLSTATE; `lock_timeout` versus `statement_timeout`;
share locks and the upgrade that conflicts; `SKIP LOCKED` skipping;
the full dequeue statement; the foreign-key lock you take without asking;
the whole compatibility matrix, built by probing; and the `LIMIT` trap.
The challenge builds a queue with visibility timeouts, retries and a
reaper. The review proves two concurrent workers never receive the same
job.
lessons.explanation:
# Reading - sql/v3d04_row_locks_queues

The useful way to hold this sector: a row lock is a **reservation you make
against the future**, and the three interesting questions are how strong
it is, what happens to somebody who wants the same row, and how long you
hold it. Almost every queue bug is a wrong answer to the third.

## Notes

**Row locks are held until the transaction ends.** There is no `UNLOCK`.
This is why the shape of your transaction *is* your lock strategy: a
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` followed by an HTTP call holds that row for the
duration of somebody else's outage. Claim, commit, then work.

**Lock strength exists to reduce false conflicts.** `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`
was added so that updating a parent row's non-key columns does not block
inserting children. If you write `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` on a row you are
only going to update a non-key column of, you have manually reintroduced
the conflict that PostgreSQL 9.3 spent effort removing.

**`NOWAIT` and `SKIP LOCKED` answer different questions.** `NOWAIT` says
"this exact row, or an error" — right for "edit this record, and tell the
user if somebody else is editing it". `SKIP LOCKED` says "any rows nobody
else has" — right for work distribution and wrong for anything where a
missing row is a wrong answer.

**A locking clause is not allowed everywhere.** `FOR UPDATE` cannot appear
with aggregates, `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `UNION`, or a window function at
the same query level; the answer is to lock in a subquery and aggregate
outside it. It also cannot lock the null-extended side of an outer join.
These are not arbitrary: locking requires identifiable base rows, and
those constructs destroy the correspondence.

**`SKIP LOCKED` skips locked rows, not invisible ones.** It has no effect
on MVCC visibility. A row inserted by an uncommitted transaction is
invisible with or without it, and a row committed after your snapshot is
invisible at `REPEATABLE READ` regardless. Queue workers should run at
`READ COMMITTED` for exactly this reason.

**Row locks and index scans interact.** Locking clauses are applied after
the plan produces rows, so a query that locks "the ten oldest ready jobs"
via an index scan locks precisely those ten. Without a supporting index —
`CREATE INDEX ON job (run_after, id) WHERE state = 'ready'` is the shape —
the scan reads and discards, and under load the queue's cost is dominated
by dead rows in the `state = 'done'` tail.

**The claim transaction and the work transaction are different
transactions.** This is the single most important structural rule in the
sector, and the one most often broken. `BEGIN; claim; call the API; mark
done; COMMIT` holds a row lock, an open snapshot and a pooled connection
for the duration of somebody else's latency. The correct shape is: one
short transaction to claim and mark `running`; the work outside any
transaction; one short transaction to mark `done` or `failed`. The price
is that a worker can die in the middle, which is what the reaper and the
`attempts` counter exist for.

**Everything here is at-least-once.** There is no arrangement of row locks
that gives exactly-once delivery, because the failure can always land
between the side effect and the acknowledgement. Accept it and make the
handler idempotent — the queue's job is to guarantee that work is not
*lost*, not that it is never repeated.

## ex1 — NOWAIT

`55P03`, `lock_not_available`. Notice it is instant: no wait, no timeout,
no ambiguity about whether the system is slow or the row is held.

## ex2 — two timeouts that are not the same

`lock_timeout` bounds how long you wait for a lock and raises `55P03`.
`statement_timeout` bounds the whole statement and raises `57014`. A
worker that must fail fast on contention but may run long needs both, and
setting only `statement_timeout` is the common mistake.

## ex3 — share locks, and the upgrade that bites

Two `FOR SHARE` holders coexist happily. The moment one of them wants
`FOR UPDATE` on the same row, it conflicts with the other's share lock —
a lock upgrade, and the classic source of deadlocks in D5. If you know you
will write, take the write lock first.

## ex4 — skipping

Three rows locked by A; B asks for three ready rows and gets the next
three. No error, no wait, no coordination. The whole queue pattern is
this one clause.

## ex5 — the dequeue statement

`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED` in a CTE, feeding an `UPDATE ...
RETURNING`. Claiming and marking in one statement means there is no window
in which the row is locked but not marked, which matters when the worker
dies.

## ex6 — the lock you did not ask for

Inserting a child row locks the parent. Under a plain `UPDATE` of a
non-key column that is fine; under an explicit `FOR UPDATE` it is not. The
lesson generalises: reaching for the strongest lock "to be safe" makes
your system less concurrent in ways that show up far from your code.

## ex7 — the matrix, by experiment

Eight probes with `NOWAIT`, each recording compatible or conflict. Building
the table yourself is worth more than reading it, because the shape you
remember afterwards is "weak locks coexist, `FOR UPDATE` excludes
everything".

## ex8 — the LIMIT trap

Zero rows returned while nine jobs wait. The cause is that `LIMIT` chose
the candidate before the lock was granted, and EvalPlanQual then
disqualified it. Every naive queue hits this, usually as "workers idle
under load".

## Further reading

- [Explicit Locking — Row-Level Locks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html#LOCKING-ROWS) — the conflict matrix, normatively.
- [SELECT — The Locking Clause](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/sql-select.html#SQL-FOR-UPDATE-SHARE) — where locking clauses are and are not permitted.
- [What is SKIP LOCKED for?](https://www.2ndquadrant.com/en/blog/what-is-select-skip-locked-for-in-postgresql-9-5/) — Craig Ringer's original write-up of the queue pattern.
- [README.tuplock](https://github.com/postgres/postgres/blob/master/src/backend/access/heap/README.tuplock) — how the four strengths are encoded in the tuple header.
lessons.fullReadme:
# V3·D4 — Row locks, SKIP LOCKED and queue tables (archive)

## Concepts

### The compatibility matrix

Rows are what a transaction already holds; columns are what another
transaction is requesting.

|                    | KEY SHARE | SHARE | NO KEY UPDATE | UPDATE |
|--------------------|-----------|-------|---------------|--------|
| **FOR KEY SHARE**  | ok        | ok    | ok            | block  |
| **FOR SHARE**      | ok        | ok    | block         | block  |
| **FOR NO KEY UPDATE** | ok     | block | block         | block  |
| **FOR UPDATE**     | block     | block | block         | block  |

Two rules generate the whole table. `FOR UPDATE` conflicts with
everything, including itself. Everything else conflicts only with modes
that would invalidate what it is protecting: a key-share lock cares only
about the key changing, a share lock cares about any column changing.

Implicit acquisitions worth memorising:

- `UPDATE` of a non-key column → `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`
- `UPDATE` of a key column, or `DELETE` → `FOR UPDATE`
- `INSERT`/`UPDATE` of a child row → `FOR KEY SHARE` on the parent

### Timeouts and their SQLSTATEs

```sql
SET lock_timeout      = '300ms';   -- 55P03 lock_not_available
SET statement_timeout = '30s';     -- 57014 query_canceled
SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';   -- terminates the session
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;      -- 55P03, immediately
```

Set them with `SET LOCAL` inside a transaction so they revert at commit —
essential behind a pooler, where a plain `SET` leaks to the next tenant of
the connection.

### The dequeue statement, annotated

```sql
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id
    FROM job
   WHERE state = 'ready'
     AND run_after <= now()          -- delayed and backed-off jobs excluded
   ORDER BY run_after, id            -- fairness; also a stable lock order
   LIMIT 5                           -- bounded batch
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED            -- exclusive, and never queue behind a peer
)
UPDATE job j
   SET state     = 'running',
       locked_at = now(),
       locked_by = $1,
       attempts  = attempts + 1
  FROM claimed c
 WHERE j.id = c.id
RETURNING j.id, j.payload;
```

The supporting index is not optional under load:

```sql
CREATE INDEX job_ready_idx ON job (run_after, id) WHERE state = 'ready';
```

A partial index on the ready subset stays small no matter how large the
completed tail grows, which is the difference between a queue that scales
and one that degrades every week until somebody deletes history.

### Reaping and retrying

```sql
-- a worker died: its jobs are still 'running' with an old locked_at
UPDATE job
   SET state = 'ready', locked_by = NULL, locked_at = NULL,
       run_after = now() + (interval '1 second' * power(2, attempts))
 WHERE state = 'running'
   AND locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes'
   AND attempts < 5;

UPDATE job SET state = 'failed'
 WHERE state = 'running' AND locked_at < now() - interval '5 minutes'
   AND attempts >= 5;
```

`power(2, attempts)` is exponential backoff; add jitter in production so a
thundering herd of retries does not re-synchronise.

### Watching a lock wait

While a block is waiting, the whole picture is in two catalog views:

```sql
SELECT a.pid,
       a.state,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by,
       left(a.query, 60)       AS q
  FROM pg_stat_activity a
 WHERE cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) > 0;

SELECT pid, locktype, relation::regclass, page, tuple,
       transactionid, mode, granted
  FROM pg_locks
 WHERE NOT granted;
```

A row-lock wait shows up as two entries, and the pair is the signature to
recognise: an ungranted `tuple` lock (the queue position for that specific
row) plus an ungranted `transactionid` lock in `ShareLock` mode on the
holder's transaction id. The waiter is literally waiting for the other
transaction to end, which is why there is no way to release a row lock
early.

`pg_blocking_pids()` is the shortcut worth memorising: hand it a pid, get
back the pids it is waiting on. It is the first query to run in any
"everything is stuck" incident, and it is also how the deadlock reports in
D5 are assembled.

### Interactive editing versus work distribution

The two everyday uses of row locks want opposite refusal behaviour:

```sql
-- "somebody else is editing this record"
SELECT * FROM document WHERE id = $1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;

-- "give me work nobody else has"
SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready'
 ORDER BY id LIMIT 10 FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;
```

Swapping them produces two classic bugs: a user-facing form that hangs for
thirty seconds, and a queue whose workers idle under load. The question to
ask is whether a *missing row* is an acceptable answer. For a queue it is
the answer; everywhere else it is a lie.

## Common mistakes

1. **Holding the claim across the work.** `BEGIN; claim; do the work;
   COMMIT` holds the row lock for the whole job and blocks the reaper.
   Claim in one short transaction, work outside it, mark done in another.
2. **`FOR UPDATE` without `SKIP LOCKED` in a queue.** Workers serialise
   behind one row, and the `LIMIT` trap makes them return empty-handed.
3. **No index on the ready predicate.** The queue slows down in proportion
   to history, not to backlog.
4. **Never deleting or partitioning completed jobs.** The table bloats,
   the index bloats, autovacuum falls behind on the hottest table you own.
5. **`SKIP LOCKED` in a non-queue query.** Silently returning fewer rows
   is a correctness bug everywhere except work distribution.
6. **Using `FOR UPDATE` where `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` would do.** You block
   every insert of a child row for no reason.
7. **`SET lock_timeout` without `SET LOCAL` behind a pooler.** The setting
   leaks to unrelated queries on the same physical connection.
8. **Assuming the claim is at-most-once.** A worker can die between claim
   and completion. Design the job to be idempotent — which is D6 — or
   accept at-least-once.

## The interview answer

> *"How would you implement a job queue in PostgreSQL?"*

A table with a state column and a partial index on the ready predicate,
and a single statement per claim: a CTE that selects the next N ready rows
`ORDER BY run_after, id LIMIT N FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, feeding an
`UPDATE ... RETURNING` that marks them running and stamps the worker and
time. `SKIP LOCKED` is what makes it scale: workers never queue behind one
another. The claim transaction is short and the actual work happens
outside it, so a row lock is never held across a network call. Delivery is
at-least-once — a worker can die after claiming — so a reaper resets
`running` rows whose `locked_at` is older than the visibility timeout,
with exponential backoff on `run_after` and a dead-letter state past a
retry cap, and the jobs themselves must be idempotent. Completed rows get
deleted or partitioned away, because the queue's real enemy is the dead
tuples in its own tail.

## Check yourself

1. Name the four row-lock strengths from weakest to strongest.
2. Which lock does an `INSERT` into a child table take on the parent row,
   and which parent operations does it block?
3. What SQLSTATE does `NOWAIT` raise? `lock_timeout`?
   `statement_timeout`?
4. Why can PostgreSQL lock millions of rows without lock-memory pressure,
   and what does it pay instead?
5. Why does `SELECT ... ORDER BY id LIMIT 1 FOR UPDATE` return zero rows
   under contention while rows are available?
6. When is `SKIP LOCKED` the wrong tool?
7. Where may a locking clause not appear, and why?
8. Write the index that keeps a queue table fast as history grows.
9. What is a multixact and what creates one?
10. Two sessions hold `FOR SHARE` on a row and both want `FOR UPDATE`.
    What happens?
11. Why should the claim and the work be in different transactions?
12. Your queue delivers some jobs twice. Name two mechanisms that could
    cause it and the property that makes it acceptable.
lessons.fullReading:
# Long read — the queue you already own

Every few years a team discovers that their message broker and their
database disagree about whether something happened, and someone proposes
moving the queue into PostgreSQL. They are usually right, and the reason
is not performance.

## Why a database queue is attractive

The decisive property is that enqueueing can share a transaction with the
work that caused it. If a user signs up and you must send a welcome
email, the row in `users` and the row in `job` commit together or not at
all. With an external broker they cannot: you either publish before
committing (and send email for a signup that rolled back) or after (and
lose the email if the process dies in between). The standard remedy — the
transactional outbox — is a queue table with a relay, which is to say you
were going to build this anyway.

The second property is that the queue is queryable. "How many jobs are
backed up, by type, older than five minutes" is a `GROUP BY`. Retrying a
specific customer's failed jobs is an `UPDATE`. Neither is easy in a
broker.

## What it costs

The cost is dead tuples, and it is not small. Every claim updates a row;
every completion updates it again; every reap updates it again. A queue
processing a million jobs a day generates several million dead tuples a
day in one small table, and that table is also the hottest thing in your
database. Autovacuum must keep up, or the partial index degrades and the
claim query starts scanning pages full of ghosts.

The mitigations, in the order you should reach for them: raise the
table's autovacuum aggressiveness
(`ALTER TABLE job SET (autovacuum_vacuum_scale_factor = 0.01,
autovacuum_vacuum_cost_delay = 0)`); delete completed rows promptly rather
than keeping them "for auditing" in the same table; give the table a
`fillfactor` below 100 so HOT updates can reuse space in place; and if the
volume justifies it, partition by day and drop whole partitions, which
turns cleanup into a catalog operation.

`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` also writes. A claim query that locks five rows
dirties up to five pages and writes WAL for each. This is invisible in the
code and very visible in the WAL volume of a busy queue.

## SKIP LOCKED's history and its relatives

Oracle had `SKIP LOCKED` — undocumented at first — for many years, and
used it inside Advanced Queuing. PostgreSQL gained it in 9.5 (2016), which
is recent enough that plenty of queue implementations in the wild predate
it and use advisory locks instead (D7) or, worse, a `SELECT` followed by a
conditional `UPDATE` with a retry loop. If you inherit one of those, the
migration is usually a single statement.

The clause is deliberately narrow: it applies only to row locks, only to
rows the scan has already produced, and it never waits. That narrowness is
what makes it safe. A common misunderstanding is that `SKIP LOCKED`
somehow relaxes isolation; it does not touch visibility at all. Rows
invisible to your snapshot are invisible either way, which is why queue
workers should run at `READ COMMITTED` — at `REPEATABLE READ` a worker's
snapshot would freeze at the first claim and it would never see newly
enqueued work.

## Performance notes

Throughput of the claim statement is dominated by index maintenance and
WAL, not by locking. Batching helps enormously: claiming ten jobs in one
statement costs barely more than claiming one, and cuts round trips by a
factor of ten. Past a few dozen workers on a single queue table, the
bottleneck becomes page contention on the hot end of the index — every
worker wants the oldest rows — and the standard remedies are to shard the
queue by a hash of a key, or to add randomness to the claim (`ORDER BY
random()` is a bad idea; `WHERE hashint8(id) % $workers = $me` is a
better one).

Beware the interaction with long transactions. A single reporting query
holding an old snapshot prevents vacuum from cleaning the queue's dead
tuples, and a queue table degrades far faster than an ordinary table when
that happens. If your queue mysteriously slows every morning at nine, look
for the analyst, not the workers. Sector D8 is that story.

## The four states a job can be in, and the fifth

A queue's state machine looks like `ready → running → done | failed`, and
the interesting question is always what happens between `running` and the
next state. There are exactly four ways out and you must design for all of
them: the work succeeded and the worker said so; the work failed and the
worker said so; the work succeeded and the worker died before saying so;
the work never started and the worker died. The last two are
indistinguishable from outside, which is why the reaper cannot know
whether to retry — and why the handler must be idempotent rather than the
queue being clever.

The fifth state is the one people forget: `running` forever, because the
reaper's timeout is longer than anyone's patience and nobody alerts on it.
A queue without a monitoring query for "oldest `ready` row" and "count of
`running` rows older than the visibility timeout" is a queue that will
fail silently. Both are one-line `SELECT`s, which is precisely the
argument for keeping the queue in the database.

```sql
SELECT state,
       count(*),
       max(now() - run_after) FILTER (WHERE state = 'ready') AS oldest_wait
  FROM job GROUP BY state;
```

## When not to use a database queue

**When you need fan-out to many independent consumers.** This design gives
each job to one worker. Broadcast is a different problem and a broker does
it better.

**When the throughput is genuinely large.** Hundreds of thousands of jobs
per second is not what a row-per-message table is for. Tens of thousands
is comfortable; be honest about which you have, and remember that most
systems overestimate by two orders of magnitude.

**When the payloads are large.** Multi-megabyte payloads in the queue
table make every vacuum and every index scan more expensive. Store the
payload elsewhere and queue a reference.

**When the consumers cannot connect to the database.** A queue is also a
coupling decision. If the workers are third-party or live in another
security domain, an interface that is not "full SQL access to my primary"
may be worth the extra moving part.

**When ordering must be strict.** `SKIP LOCKED` explicitly gives up
ordering: a worker takes the oldest *available* job, not the oldest job. If
messages for one customer must be processed in order, you need one more
idea — partition the queue by a key and let a worker claim a whole key at
a time, or keep a per-key sequence and refuse to process out of order.
Trying to get strict global ordering out of a `SKIP LOCKED` queue by
adding workers is a contradiction in terms; the parallelism *is* the
reordering.

**When `LISTEN`/`NOTIFY` would do.** For low-latency wake-ups with no
durability requirement, notification is far cheaper than polling. The
common production shape is both: `NOTIFY` on insert so idle workers wake
immediately, plus a slow poll as a backstop, because notifications are not
delivered to a worker that was disconnected at the time.

exercises.title: Ex1
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — NOWAIT, and the code it raises

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. The simplest lock conflict, made instant.

```
-- @A  BEGIN;
--     SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- @B expect 55P03
--     SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
-- @A  COMMIT;
-- @B  BEGIN;
--     SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
--     record 'acquired_after_release' = 'yes'
--     COMMIT;
```

Without `NOWAIT`, B would sit there until A commits — which, with the
gate's `lock_timeout = '5s'`, would fail the mission with a much less
informative error. `NOWAIT` converts an unbounded wait into an immediate,
specific failure: `55P03`, `lock_not_available`, message `could not obtain
lock on row in relation "job"`.

That is the right tool for interactive work. "Somebody else is editing
this record" is a sentence you can show a user; a thirty-second spinner is
not.

The last two blocks prove the lock was the only obstacle: the identical
statement succeeds the moment A's transaction ends. There is no `UNLOCK`
in PostgreSQL — a row lock is released by `COMMIT` or `ROLLBACK` and by
nothing else.

Record with `INSERT INTO observation (label, value) VALUES
('acquired_after_release', 'yes');`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Four blocks. The `expect` block contains exactly one statement; do not add
a `COMMIT` to it, since the gate rolls that session back for you.

## Hint 2
The locking clause goes at the very end of the query, after any `ORDER BY`
and `LIMIT`:

```sql
SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
```

`NOWAIT` and `SKIP LOCKED` are alternatives — a statement may carry one or
the other, not both.

## Hint 3
The final B block needs its own `BEGIN` and `COMMIT`. Without them the
`SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` still works (it is an implicit transaction) but
the lock is released the instant the statement returns, which is a fine
thing to know and a bad habit to build.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what "row lock" means for a row nobody has written. A's `SELECT FOR
UPDATE` did not change any column, yet it dirtied the page and wrote WAL,
because the lock is stored in the tuple header. A locking read is a write.

## Hint 2
Compare the three refusal styles on the same conflict:

```sql
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;        -- 55P03, immediately
SET lock_timeout = '300ms';          -- 55P03, after 300ms
SELECT ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED;   -- no error, no row
```

Only the third one leaves your application unable to tell the difference
between "held by someone" and "does not exist".

## Hint 3
If the `expect` block passes but the final block fails, A's `COMMIT` is
probably in the wrong place — it must come after the failure and before
B's second attempt.

exercises.title: Ex2
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — two timeouts that are not the same timeout

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. `lock_timeout` and `statement_timeout` are
routinely confused, and the difference decides whether a worker fails fast
on contention or kills its own long-running work.

Session A locks job 1 and holds it. Session B then makes two attempts,
each inside a `DO` block that catches the failure and records its
`SQLSTATE`:

```
-- @A  BEGIN; SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- @B  SET lock_timeout = '300ms';
--     DO block: try  PERFORM 1 FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
--       success -> record 'lock_timeout_result' = 'acquired'
--       WHEN lock_not_available -> record 'lock_timeout_result' = SQLSTATE
--     SET lock_timeout = 0;
--     SET statement_timeout = '300ms';
--     DO block: same attempt
--       WHEN query_canceled -> record 'statement_timeout_result' = SQLSTATE
--     SET statement_timeout = 0;
-- @A  COMMIT;
```

Expected: `lock_timeout_result` = `55P03`, `statement_timeout_result` =
`57014`.

Same conflict, same wait, two different error codes — because
`lock_timeout` bounds *lock acquisition* while `statement_timeout` bounds
the *whole statement*. A background worker that may legitimately run for a
minute but must never queue behind a lock needs `lock_timeout` set low and
`statement_timeout` set high; setting only the second gives you the worst
of both.

Use `SET LOCAL` rather than `SET` when you write this for real: behind a
connection pooler a plain `SET` outlives your transaction and applies to
whoever gets the connection next.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Both attempts are identical SQL. The only difference is which GUC is
armed, which is exactly the point being measured — so make sure you
disarm the first before arming the second.

## Hint 2
Capturing a SQLSTATE in PL/pgSQL:

```sql
DO $$ BEGIN
  PERFORM 1 FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
  INSERT INTO observation (label, value) VALUES ('x', 'acquired');
EXCEPTION WHEN lock_not_available THEN
  INSERT INTO observation (label, value) VALUES ('x', SQLSTATE);
END $$;
```

`SQLSTATE` and `SQLERRM` are in scope inside the handler.

## Hint 3
`SET lock_timeout = 0;` means "no timeout" and is how you disarm it. The
condition name for `57014` is `query_canceled` — spelled with one `l`,
American style, like most PostgreSQL condition names.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict which one you would want on a web request handler. Almost always
both, and low: a request that waits three seconds for a lock has already
failed from the user's point of view, whether or not it eventually
succeeds.

## Hint 2
There is a third member of the family, and it is the one that saves
production:

```sql
SET idle_in_transaction_session_timeout = '10s';
```

It does not bound a statement at all — it terminates a session that has an
open transaction and is not running anything. Sector D8 is about what that
prevents.

## Hint 3
If `statement_timeout_result` comes back `55P03`, the `lock_timeout` from
the first attempt is still armed and won the race. Disarm it with `SET
lock_timeout = 0;` between the two blocks.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — share locks coexist, upgrades do not

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. `FOR SHARE` says "this row must not change while
I look at it". Two readers can both say that. Neither can then quietly
become a writer.

```
-- @A  BEGIN; SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE;
-- @B  BEGIN; SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE;
--     record 'share_with_share' = 'compatible'
--     COMMIT;
-- @B expect 55P03
--     SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
-- @A  COMMIT;
-- @B  BEGIN;
--     SELECT * FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE NOWAIT;
--     record 'update_after_release' = 'acquired'
--     COMMIT;
```

B commits before attempting the upgrade so that the first observation
survives — a block that fails takes its writes with it.

The middle failure is a **lock upgrade**, and it is the single most common
source of deadlocks in real systems: two transactions both hold a shared
lock on a row and both then want it exclusively, so each waits for the
other to let go. Neither ever will. D5 is about recognising that shape.

The habit that avoids it: if you know you are going to write the row, take
`FOR UPDATE` on the first read. Taking a weak lock and strengthening it
later is optimism you pay for at 3am.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Work out who B is actually waiting for in the failing block. B holds no
lock at that point — it committed. The conflict is with A's share lock,
because `FOR UPDATE` conflicts with everything, including `FOR SHARE`.

## Hint 2
The shape of a genuine upgrade deadlock, for reference:

```
-- @A  BEGIN; SELECT ... FOR SHARE;      -- both hold share
-- @B  BEGIN; SELECT ... FOR SHARE;
-- @A  SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;            -- waits for B
-- @B  SELECT ... FOR UPDATE;            -- waits for A -> deadlock
```

You will build exactly this in D5, deliberately.

## Hint 3
Six blocks. B's `COMMIT` before the `expect` block is load-bearing: keep
it, or the `share_with_share` observation disappears with the failed
transaction and the gate will tell you the label is missing.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what two share holders on one row do to `xmax`, which can hold exactly
one transaction id. The answer is a **multixact**: a separate id whose
membership list lives in `pg_multixact`. Heavy share locking therefore has
its own wraparound risk and its own SLRU contention, entirely separate
from ordinary transaction ids.

## Hint 2
`FOR SHARE` is rarer in application code than people expect, because its
usual job — "make sure this parent row still exists while I insert a
child" — is done for you by the foreign key, which takes `FOR KEY SHARE`
automatically. Ex6 makes that visible.

## Hint 3
If the `expect` block succeeds instead of failing, check that A is still
inside its transaction: A's `COMMIT` must come after the failure, not
before.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — skipping what somebody else is holding

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The clause that makes queues work, in isolation.

```
-- @A  BEGIN;
--     SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 3
--       FOR UPDATE;                       -- locks 1, 2, 3
-- @B  record 'skipped_ids' = the three ids a SKIP LOCKED claim returns
-- @A  COMMIT;
```

B's query is the same shape with two words added, wrapped so you can
aggregate the result:

```sql
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'skipped_ids', string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id)
  FROM (
    SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 3
     FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  ) s;
```

Expected value: `4,5,6`.

Note the shape: the locking clause is inside a sub-select, because `FOR
UPDATE` may not appear at the same query level as an aggregate. That is
not a quirk to work around — locking requires identifiable base rows, and
`string_agg` destroys that correspondence.

B did not wait, did not error, and did not receive the rows A is working
on. It also has no way of knowing that rows 1–3 exist. That ambiguity is
the price, and it is exactly the right trade for work distribution and
exactly the wrong one for "show me the three oldest jobs".

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Three blocks. A must still be inside its transaction when B runs, or the
locks are released and B gets 1,2,3.

## Hint 2
Why the subquery? Try it without and read the error:

```
ERROR:  FOR UPDATE is not allowed with aggregate functions
```

The same restriction applies to `GROUP BY`, `DISTINCT`, `UNION` and window
functions.

## Hint 3
`string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id)` produces `4,5,6`. The inner
`ORDER BY id LIMIT 3` decides *which* rows; the aggregate's `ORDER BY`
decides the order inside the string. Both are needed for a deterministic
answer.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict what B returns if you remove `SKIP LOCKED` but keep `NOWAIT`, and
what it returns with neither. Three different behaviours from the same
query, and only one of them is right for a worker.

## Hint 2
`SKIP LOCKED` does not touch visibility. A row that another transaction
has inserted but not committed is invisible to B with or without the
clause — MVCC already hid it. The clause only skips rows that are visible
but locked, which is why queue workers must run at `READ COMMITTED`: at
`REPEATABLE READ` a worker's snapshot would freeze and it would never see
newly enqueued jobs.

## Hint 3
If `skipped_ids` comes back `1,2,3`, A's block is missing its `BEGIN` — a
bare `SELECT ... FOR UPDATE` in autocommit releases its locks the moment
it returns.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — the dequeue statement

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Put the pieces together into the statement a real
worker runs.

Write **one statement**, with no `BEGIN`, that claims the two oldest ready
jobs whose `run_after` has arrived:

- select from `job` where `state = 'ready'` and `run_after <= now()`,
  ordered by `run_after, id`, limited to 2, locked `FOR UPDATE SKIP
  LOCKED`, in a CTE named `claimed`;
- from that CTE, `UPDATE job` setting `state = 'running'`, `locked_at =
  now()`, `locked_by = 'worker-1'`, `attempts = attempts + 1`;
- and record the claimed ids into `observation` as label `claimed_ids`,
  comma-separated in ascending order.

Expected `claimed_ids`: `1,2`. Afterwards jobs 1 and 2 must be `running`
with `attempts = 1` and `locked_by = 'worker-1'`, and jobs 3–10 must be
untouched.

Three structural points are worth stating out loud.

The claim and the mark happen in **one statement**, so there is no window
in which a row is locked but not marked. If the worker dies immediately
after, the row is `running` with a `locked_at` a reaper can find, rather
than `ready` and locked by a connection that is about to disappear.

The `LIMIT` sits inside the CTE, before the locking clause is applied to
those rows — this is safe here precisely because `SKIP LOCKED` means the
scan keeps going past locked rows rather than queueing behind them. Ex8
shows the same shape without `SKIP LOCKED`, where it is not safe at all.

And `attempts = attempts + 1` is incremented at *claim* time, not at
failure time, so a job that crashes the worker before it can report
anything still counts against the retry budget. A poison message that
kills its worker must not be retried forever.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The statement has three parts: a CTE that picks and locks, an `UPDATE`
joined to it, and an aggregation of what the update returned. Sketch the
three before writing any of them.

## Hint 2
Chaining a data-modifying CTE into an aggregate insert:

```sql
WITH claimed AS ( ... FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED ),
     upd AS (
       UPDATE job j SET ... FROM claimed c WHERE j.id = c.id RETURNING j.id
     )
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'claimed_ids', string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id) FROM upd;
```

## Hint 3
Clause order inside the CTE is `WHERE`, `ORDER BY`, `LIMIT`, then the
locking clause last. Writing `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED LIMIT 2` is a syntax
error, and it is the mistake everyone makes once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what the worker does next, and how long this transaction lasts. The
answer that matters: this statement is the *whole* claim transaction. The
work happens afterwards, outside it, because a row lock held across a job
is a row lock held across whatever that job talks to.

## Hint 2
The index that makes this statement stay fast as the table grows:

```sql
CREATE INDEX job_ready_idx ON job (run_after, id) WHERE state = 'ready';
```

A partial index on the ready subset does not grow with completed history —
which is the difference between a queue that scales and one that gets
slower every week until somebody notices the table is 40 GB.

## Hint 3
If your `UPDATE` touches more than two rows, the join to `claimed` is
missing or wrong: `FROM claimed c WHERE j.id = c.id` is what restricts it.
A `FROM` clause with no matching `WHERE` is a cross join, and here that
would claim the entire queue.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3d04_row_locks_queues / ex5 — claim and mark in a single statement
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id
    FROM job
   WHERE state = 'ready'
     AND run_after <= now()
   ORDER BY run_after, id
   LIMIT 2
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
), upd AS (
  UPDATE job j
     SET state     = 'running',
         locked_at = now(),
         locked_by = 'worker-1',
         attempts  = j.attempts + 1
    FROM claimed c
   WHERE j.id = c.id
  RETURNING j.id
)
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'claimed_ids', string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id) FROM upd;

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — the lock you take without asking

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. `payment.account_id` references `account.id`.
Inserting a payment therefore has to be sure the parent row will still be
there, so it takes `FOR KEY SHARE` on it — a lock you never wrote.

Phase 1 — a plain update of a non-key column:

```
-- @A  BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 1 WHERE id = 1;
-- @B  INSERT INTO payment (account_id, amount) VALUES (1, 10.00);
--     record 'insert_under_nonkey_update' = 'succeeded'
-- @A  COMMIT;
```

It works. `UPDATE` of a non-key column takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, which is
compatible with `FOR KEY SHARE`. Before PostgreSQL 9.3 there was no such
distinction and this insert blocked — a notorious source of contention on
popular parent rows.

Phase 2 — the same insert against an explicitly `FOR UPDATE`-locked
parent:

```
-- @A  BEGIN; SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE;
-- @B  SET lock_timeout = '300ms';
-- @B expect 55P03
--     INSERT INTO payment (account_id, amount) VALUES (2, 10.00);
-- @A  COMMIT;
```

`FOR UPDATE` conflicts with everything, so the child insert waits and then
times out.

The lesson is about defaults. Reaching for `FOR UPDATE` "to be safe" on a
row you are only going to update a non-key column of re-creates a
bottleneck the database went to some trouble to remove — and it shows up
as latency in a completely different part of the system, on inserts
nobody thought were related to your code.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Name the two locks in phase 1 before running it: what does A's `UPDATE`
take on `account` id 1, and what does B's `INSERT` need on the same row?
The compatibility answer follows immediately.

## Hint 2
The lock a foreign key takes is visible in the wait, not in the SQL. To
see the whole picture during phase 2, another session could run:

```sql
SELECT pid, locktype, relation::regclass, mode, granted FROM pg_locks
 WHERE NOT granted;
```

A row-lock wait appears as a `tuple` lock plus a `transactionid` lock on
the holder's id.

## Hint 3
Six blocks. `SET lock_timeout` must be in its own B block *before* the
`expect` block — a `SET` inside a block that the gate rolls back may not
survive, and without the timeout the insert waits for the gate's full five
seconds and fails with the wrong error.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask which columns count as "key" columns. Any column covered by a unique
index that a foreign key could reference — in practice the primary key.
`UPDATE account SET id = ...` takes the strong lock; `UPDATE account SET
balance = ...` does not. This is why renaming a primary key is a much
bigger event than it looks.

## Hint 2
The same effect makes a busy parent row a system-wide bottleneck:

```sql
-- 'default' tenant row, referenced by ten million child rows
SELECT * FROM tenant WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;   -- blocks every child insert
```

If you need to serialise something around a parent, an advisory lock (D7)
does it without touching the row and without blocking foreign keys.

## Hint 3
If phase 2's insert succeeds, check that A used `FOR UPDATE` and not `FOR
NO KEY UPDATE`, and that A's transaction is still open — `COMMIT` belongs
in the last block.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — build the compatibility matrix by experiment

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. Rather than reading the table in the manual,
probe it.

Session A holds one lock; session B tries all four strengths with
`NOWAIT`, each inside its own `DO` block so a successful probe releases
its lock immediately and does not contaminate the next one. Each probe
records `compatible` or `conflict`.

Phase 1 — A holds `FOR KEY SHARE` on job 1. Record:

| label                       | expected     |
|-----------------------------|--------------|
| `keyshare_vs_keyshare`      | `compatible` |
| `keyshare_vs_share`         | `compatible` |
| `keyshare_vs_nokeyupdate`   | `compatible` |
| `keyshare_vs_update`        | `conflict`   |

Phase 2 — A holds `FOR UPDATE` on job 2. Record `update_vs_keyshare`,
`update_vs_share`, `update_vs_nokeyupdate`, `update_vs_update`; all four
are `conflict`.

Each probe looks like:

```sql
DO $$ BEGIN
  PERFORM 1 FROM job WHERE id = 1 FOR SHARE NOWAIT;
  INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
  VALUES ('keyshare_vs_share', 'compatible');
EXCEPTION WHEN lock_not_available THEN
  INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
  VALUES ('keyshare_vs_share', 'conflict');
END $$;
```

Eight probes, two A blocks. The shape that should stay in your memory
afterwards: **weak locks coexist; `FOR UPDATE` excludes everything,
including another `FOR UPDATE`**. Everything between those poles conflicts
only with modes that would invalidate what it protects — a key-share lock
cares only about the key, a share lock about any column.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Why one `DO` block per probe rather than one block with four attempts? A
successful lock is held until its transaction ends, and a `DO` block is
one statement, therefore one transaction. Separate blocks give each probe
a clean slate.

## Hint 2
The four locking clauses, spelled exactly:

```sql
FOR KEY SHARE NOWAIT
FOR SHARE NOWAIT
FOR NO KEY UPDATE NOWAIT
FOR UPDATE NOWAIT
```

`NOWAIT` always comes last.

## Hint 3
Ten blocks in total: A locks, four B probes, A commits, A locks again,
four more B probes, A commits. Keeping the labels exactly as the table
spells them is what lets the gate check all eight at once.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict all eight before you run them, then count how many you got wrong.
Most people miss `keyshare_vs_nokeyupdate` — it feels like it should
conflict, and the fact that it does not is precisely what stops parent
updates from blocking child inserts.

## Hint 2
The matrix is generated by two sentences, which is easier to carry than
sixteen cells:

- `FOR UPDATE` conflicts with every mode, including itself.
- Every other pair conflicts only if one of them would change what the
  other is protecting — the key, for key-share; any column, for share.

## Hint 3
Phase 2 needs A's first transaction committed before the second begins,
or A will be holding both locks and phase 1's row will still be involved.
One `COMMIT` between the phases.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — the claim that returns nothing while ten jobs wait

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The trap every naive queue falls into, reproduced
on purpose.

Phase 1 — `FOR UPDATE` with a `LIMIT` and no `SKIP LOCKED`:

```
-- @A        BEGIN;
--           UPDATE job SET state = 'running'
--            WHERE id = (SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready'
--                        ORDER BY id LIMIT 1);
-- @B async  record 'blocking_claim_rows' = how many rows this returns:
--           SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
--             FOR UPDATE;
-- @A        COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'ready_left' = count(*) FROM job WHERE state = 'ready'
```

Expected: `blocking_claim_rows` = `0`, `ready_left` = `9`.

B waited, was granted the lock, and then got nothing — while nine ready
jobs sat untouched. The mechanism is the one from D3's ex7: `LIMIT 1`
chose the candidate *before* the lock was granted, and when B unblocked,
EvalPlanQual re-checked `state = 'ready'` against A's new version, found
`running`, and dropped the row. There is no second candidate to fall back
to, because the `LIMIT` already discarded them.

In production this is "workers go idle under load", and it gets diagnosed
as everything except what it is.

Phase 2 — the fix, one clause:

```
-- @A        BEGIN;
--           UPDATE job SET state = 'running' WHERE id = 2;
-- @B        record 'skip_locked_claim' = the id returned by the same query
--           with FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
-- @A        COMMIT;
```

Expected: `skip_locked_claim` = `3` (job 1 is already `running` from phase
1, job 2 is locked by A, so the first *ready and unlocked* row is 3).

Record counts and ids by wrapping the locking query in a sub-select, as in
ex4.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Before running phase 1, say out loud what B's query is asking for: "the
first ready row, and lock it". By the time B is allowed to look, is its
chosen row still ready? Is B allowed to change its mind about which row it
wanted?

## Hint 2
Counting rows a locking query returned:

```sql
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'blocking_claim_rows', count(*)::text
  FROM (SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 1
         FOR UPDATE) s;
```

The aggregate has to be outside the locking sub-select.

## Hint 3
Phase 1's B block must be `async`, because it genuinely blocks until A
commits. Put `-- @join` after A's `COMMIT` and before any observation that
depends on B having finished.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask why `SKIP LOCKED` does not have the same problem. Because it never
blocks: the scan simply passes over the locked row and keeps looking, so
the `LIMIT` is filled from rows that are actually available. The predicate
is evaluated during the scan, not re-evaluated after a wait.

## Hint 2
There is a second, subtler version of this bug that `SKIP LOCKED` does not
fix:

```sql
UPDATE job SET state = 'running'
 WHERE id IN (SELECT id FROM job WHERE state = 'ready' ORDER BY id LIMIT 5);
```

Two workers can select the same five ids and one will simply overwrite the
other's claim, because nothing locked anything. The `FOR UPDATE` is not
decoration — without it there is no claim at all, only a race.

## Hint 3
If phase 1's `blocking_claim_rows` comes back `1`, A's `UPDATE` did not
lock job 1 before B looked — check that A's block has `BEGIN` and that B's
block carries the `async` marker so it starts while A is still open.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — a queue that survives a dead worker

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. Build the whole thing: claiming, a
visibility timeout, exponential backoff, and a dead-letter state.

Write two functions and then exercise them.

**1. `claim_jobs(p_worker text, p_n int) RETURNS TABLE (id bigint,
payload text)`** — the dequeue statement from ex5, parameterised:
`state = 'ready'` and `run_after <= now()`, ordered by `run_after, id`,
limited to `p_n`, `FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED`, updating the claimed rows to
`running` with `locked_at = now()`, `locked_by = p_worker`, `attempts =
attempts + 1`, and returning id and payload.

**2. `reap_stale(p_timeout interval, p_max_attempts int) RETURNS int`** —
finds rows still `running` whose `locked_at` is older than `p_timeout`
and:

- returns them to `ready` with `locked_by` and `locked_at` cleared and
  `run_after = now() + interval '1 second' * power(2, attempts)` when
  `attempts < p_max_attempts`;
- moves them to `failed` when `attempts >= p_max_attempts`;
- returns the total number of rows it touched.

Then this interleaving:

```
-- @A  SELECT * FROM claim_jobs('worker-a', 2);       -- claims 1, 2
-- @B  SELECT * FROM claim_jobs('worker-b', 2);       -- claims 3, 4
-- @A  UPDATE job SET state='done' WHERE id = 1;      -- worker A finishes one
--     -- and then dies: job 2 stays 'running' forever
-- @A  UPDATE job SET locked_at = now() - interval '10 minutes'
--      WHERE id IN (2, 3, 4);                        -- simulate elapsed time
-- @A  UPDATE job SET attempts = 5 WHERE id = 4;      -- job 4 has used its budget
-- @A  record 'reaped' = reap_stale('5 minutes', 5)::text
-- @A  record 'state_2' / 'state_3' / 'state_4' = each job's state
--     record 'backoff_2' = (run_after > now())::text
```

Expected: `reaped` = `3`, `state_2` = `ready`, `state_3` = `ready`,
`state_4` = `failed`, `backoff_2` = `true`.

Note the two design decisions the gate is checking. `attempts` is
incremented at *claim* time, so a job that kills its worker before
reporting anything still burns a retry — otherwise a poison message loops
forever. And the reaper works off `locked_at`, not off any liveness signal
from the worker, because a dead worker cannot tell you it is dead.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Both functions are single statements wrapped in `RETURN QUERY` /
`RETURN`. Resist writing loops: the claim is one CTE-plus-`UPDATE`, and
the reaper is one `UPDATE` with a `CASE` deciding the target state.

## Hint 2
A `CASE` in the `SET` list handles both reaper outcomes at once:

```sql
UPDATE job
   SET state = CASE WHEN attempts >= p_max_attempts THEN 'failed'
                    ELSE 'ready' END,
       run_after = CASE WHEN attempts >= p_max_attempts THEN run_after
                        ELSE now() + interval '1 second' * power(2, attempts)
                   END,
       ...
 WHERE state = 'running' AND locked_at < now() - p_timeout
RETURNING 1;
```

Then count the returned rows with `GET DIAGNOSTICS n = ROW_COUNT` or by
wrapping in a CTE.

## Hint 3
`power(2, attempts)` returns `double precision`; multiplying an interval
by it is fine, but the whole expression needs `interval '1 second' *
power(2, attempts)` in that order. For the function returning a set, the
signature is `RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, payload text)` and the body is
`RETURN QUERY WITH claimed AS (...) UPDATE ... RETURNING j.id, j.payload;`
