— qualify the returned columns or they collide with the `TABLE` output
parameter names.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Work out what happens if the reaper runs while a healthy worker is still
holding a claimed row. Nothing good: the job would be handed to a second
worker while the first is still running it. That is why the timeout must
be comfortably longer than the slowest legitimate job, and why long jobs
should heartbeat by bumping `locked_at`.

## Hint 2
The delivery guarantee you have built is **at-least-once**, and it cannot
be anything else — a worker can always die between finishing the work and
marking the row done. The consequence is not a queue problem, it is a job
design problem: every handler must be idempotent, which is exactly what
sector D6 constructs.

## Hint 3
If `reaped` comes back `4`, job 1 was included — check the reaper's
`WHERE state = 'running'`, since job 1 is `done`. If `backoff_2` is
`false`, the `run_after` arithmetic ran on a row whose `attempts` was 0;
remember the claim already incremented it to 1.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3d04_row_locks_queues / challenge — claim, visibility timeout, backoff
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION claim_jobs(p_worker text, p_n int)
RETURNS TABLE (id bigint, payload text)
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
BEGIN
  RETURN QUERY
  WITH claimed AS (
    SELECT j.id
      FROM job j
     WHERE j.state = 'ready'
       AND j.run_after <= now()
     ORDER BY j.run_after, j.id
     LIMIT p_n
     FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
  )
  UPDATE job j
     SET state     = 'running',
         locked_at = now(),
         locked_by = p_worker,
         attempts  = j.attempts + 1
    FROM claimed c
   WHERE j.id = c.id
  RETURNING j.id, j.payload;
END $$;

CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION reap_stale(p_timeout interval, p_max_attempts int)
RETURNS int
LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$
DECLARE
  touched int;
BEGIN
  UPDATE job j
     SET state = CASE WHEN j.attempts >= p_max_attempts THEN 'failed'
                      ELSE 'ready' END,
         run_after = CASE WHEN j.attempts >= p_max_attempts THEN j.run_after
                          ELSE now() + interval '1 second' * power(2, j.attempts)
                     END,
         locked_by = NULL,
         locked_at = NULL
   WHERE j.state = 'running'
     AND j.locked_at < now() - p_timeout;

  GET DIAGNOSTICS touched = ROW_COUNT;
  RETURN touched;
END $$;

-- @A
SELECT * FROM claim_jobs('worker-a', 2);

-- @B
SELECT * FROM claim_jobs('worker-b', 2);

-- @A
UPDATE job SET state = 'done' WHERE id = 1;

-- @A
-- Worker A died holding job 2; workers B's jobs are also now stale.
UPDATE job SET locked_at = now() - interval '10 minutes' WHERE id IN (2, 3, 4);
UPDATE job SET attempts = 5 WHERE id = 4;

-- @A
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
VALUES ('reaped', reap_stale(interval '5 minutes', 5)::text);

INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'state_2', state FROM job WHERE id = 2;
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'state_3', state FROM job WHERE id = 3;
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'state_4', state FROM job WHERE id = 4;
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'backoff_2', (run_after > now())::text FROM job WHERE id = 2;

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — prove there is no double delivery

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. A different angle: instead of building the
claim, *verify* it. Two workers claim concurrently, and you assert the
property that matters.

Run two genuinely concurrent claims with the `async` marker, each taking
three jobs and recording the ids it received:

```
-- @A async   claim 3 jobs as 'worker-a', record 'worker_a' = ids, comma-separated
-- @B async   claim 3 jobs as 'worker-b', record 'worker_b' = ids
-- @join
-- @A         record 'claimed_total'  = count(*) FROM job WHERE state = 'running'
--            record 'overlap'        = number of jobs claimed by both (expect 0)
--            record 'ready_left'     = count(*) FROM job WHERE state = 'ready'
```

Each claim is the ex5 statement with `LIMIT 3`, `locked_by` set to the
worker's name, and the returned ids aggregated with `string_agg(id::text,
',' ORDER BY id)`.

Expected: `claimed_total` = `6`, `overlap` = `0`, `ready_left` = `4`.

Which worker gets which ids is **not determined** — that is the honest
part of this exercise. Under real concurrency the interleaving varies, so
the gate checks the properties that must hold rather than a fixed answer:
six jobs claimed, no job claimed twice, four left. Concurrency tests that
assert exact orderings are tests that fail on a slow morning.

Compute `overlap` as the number of `job` rows whose id appears in both
recorded lists — the simplest form is to count rows where `locked_by` is
neither `'worker-a'` nor `'worker-b'`, which must be zero among running
rows, together with a check that the two lists share no element:

```sql
SELECT count(*) FROM (
  SELECT unnest(string_to_array(value, ',')) AS id FROM observation
   WHERE label = 'worker_a'
  INTERSECT
  SELECT unnest(string_to_array(value, ',')) FROM observation
   WHERE label = 'worker_b'
) x;
```

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d04_row_locks_queues review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The property under test is disjointness, not identity. Write the assertion
first — "these two sets do not intersect" — and the rest of the file
follows.

## Hint 2
`string_to_array(value, ',')` turns `'1,2,3'` back into an array, and
`unnest` turns that into rows. `INTERSECT` between two such sets is the
whole overlap check.

## Hint 3
Both claim blocks must carry `async`, and `-- @join` must come before any
block that reads the results. Without the join you may observe a queue
where only one worker has finished, which looks like a failure and is
actually a race in the test rather than in the code.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what would make this test fail. Removing `SKIP LOCKED` would not
produce overlap — it would produce a worker returning zero rows, per ex8.
Removing `FOR UPDATE` entirely *would* produce overlap, because then
nothing prevents two workers from selecting the same ids and both updating
them. Try it once, locally, to see the failure you are guarding against.

## Hint 2
This is the shape of a good concurrency test in general: run the real
statements concurrently, then assert invariants — disjointness,
conservation, monotonicity — rather than expected outputs. The same
discipline applies to the transfer in D1 (money is conserved) and the
on-call roster in D3 (at least one remains).

## Hint 3
If `claimed_total` is 3 rather than 6, one async block failed silently —
check that both claims use different `locked_by` values and that neither
one exceeded the ten available jobs.

references.solution.sql:
-- v3d04_row_locks_queues / review1 — two workers, no job delivered twice
-- @A async
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM job
   WHERE state = 'ready' AND run_after <= now()
   ORDER BY run_after, id
   LIMIT 3
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
), upd AS (
  UPDATE job j
     SET state = 'running', locked_at = now(), locked_by = 'worker-a',
         attempts = j.attempts + 1
    FROM claimed c
   WHERE j.id = c.id
  RETURNING j.id
)
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'worker_a', coalesce(string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id), '') FROM upd;

-- @B async
WITH claimed AS (
  SELECT id FROM job
   WHERE state = 'ready' AND run_after <= now()
   ORDER BY run_after, id
   LIMIT 3
   FOR UPDATE SKIP LOCKED
), upd AS (
  UPDATE job j
     SET state = 'running', locked_at = now(), locked_by = 'worker-b',
         attempts = j.attempts + 1
    FROM claimed c
   WHERE j.id = c.id
  RETURNING j.id
)
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'worker_b', coalesce(string_agg(id::text, ',' ORDER BY id), '') FROM upd;

-- @join

-- @A
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'claimed_total', count(*)::text FROM job WHERE state = 'running';

INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'overlap', count(*)::text FROM (
  SELECT unnest(string_to_array(value, ',')) AS id FROM observation
   WHERE label = 'worker_a'
  INTERSECT
  SELECT unnest(string_to_array(value, ',')) FROM observation
   WHERE label = 'worker_b'
) x;

INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
SELECT 'ready_left', count(*)::text FROM job WHERE state = 'ready';

lessons.title: V3·D5 — Deadlocks: causes, logs, and write ordering
lessons.summary: A deadlock is not a database fault, it is a write-ordering bug with a specific shape. You will build four of them on purpose — updates, unique-index inserts, foreign keys, lock upgrades — read the report the server produces, time how long detection costs, and then remove the cycle with a canonical lock order.
lessons.briefing:
# V3·D5 — Deadlocks: causes, logs, and write ordering

D4 gave you row locks and ended on a hint: two transactions that hold
shared locks and both want to upgrade will wait for each other forever.
This sector is about that "forever", which in PostgreSQL lasts about one
second and then somebody dies.

A deadlock is a cycle in the "who is waiting for whom" graph. Nothing is
broken when one happens — no data is corrupted, no lock leaks, the victim
is rolled back completely. What a deadlock tells you is that two code
paths acquire the same set of locks in different orders, and that is
always fixable, usually in one line.

## The mechanism

When a transaction waits for a lock, it sets a timer of `deadlock_timeout`
(one second by default). If the lock is granted first, nothing happens and
you never knew. If the timer fires, that backend walks the wait graph
looking for a cycle that includes itself. If it finds one, it **cancels
itself**:

```
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 4312 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8891;
         blocked by process 4287.
         Process 4287 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8894;
         blocked by process 4312.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,3) in relation "account"
SQLSTATE: 40P01
```

Read that report as a directed graph. Each `Process X waits for … blocked
by process Y` is one edge; if the edges form a loop you have the cycle,
and the *last* process listed is the victim. `ShareLock on transaction
N` means "waiting for transaction N to end", which is what waiting for a
row lock actually looks like — you wait on the holder's transaction id,
not on the row.

Two settings turn this from folklore into evidence. `log_lock_waits = on`
logs any wait longer than `deadlock_timeout` along with the blocking pid,
so you see the *near*-deadlocks too. `deadlock_timeout` itself is the
detection latency: every deadlock costs at least that much wall clock, on
both sides, which is why a system with frequent deadlocks is slow before
it is wrong.

## The four common shapes

**Opposite update order.** A updates account 1 then 2; B updates 2 then 1.
The textbook case, and the one your transfer function creates the day
somebody transfers money in both directions at once.

**Unique-index insertion.** Two transactions insert the same key. The
second one waits on the first's transaction id — no explicit lock, no
`FOR UPDATE`, just `INSERT`. Two batch loaders inserting overlapping tags
in different orders deadlock without a single lock statement between
them.

**Foreign keys.** Inserting a child takes `FOR KEY SHARE` on the parent.
If one path locks parent 1 explicitly and inserts a child of parent 2,
while another does the reverse, the cycle runs through rows in two
different tables — which is much harder to spot in review.

**Lock upgrades.** Two transactions hold `FOR SHARE` on the same row and
both then want `FOR UPDATE`. One row, no ordering mistake, and still a
deadlock. The rule that avoids it: if you might write, take the write lock
on the first read.

## The fix, and the non-fixes

The fix is a **canonical order**: every code path that touches a set of
rows acquires them in the same deterministic sequence. Ascending primary
key is the usual choice because it needs no coordination — `least()` and
`greatest()` for two rows, `ORDER BY id` for many.

```sql
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = least(p_from, p_to)    FOR UPDATE;
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = greatest(p_from, p_to) FOR UPDATE;
```

The order must span *tables* too: if any path locks a summary row and an
account row, every path must take them in the same order.

The non-fixes are worth naming. Retrying works and is necessary, but it
treats the symptom; a system that deadlocks constantly and retries
constantly is spending `deadlock_timeout` per attempt. Raising the
isolation level does nothing — `SERIALIZABLE` adds serialization failures,
it does not remove lock cycles. Lowering `deadlock_timeout` makes
detection faster and the wait-graph checks more frequent, which is a
throughput trade, not a fix.

## Markers, extended

D2 and D3's interleaving format, with two additions used heavily here:

- Markers combine: `-- @B async expect 40P01` starts a block without
  waiting *and* requires it to fail with that SQLSTATE. An async block's
  expectation is checked at `-- @join`.
- Before starting the next block, the gate waits until an async session is
  either finished or genuinely **blocked on a lock**. That removes the
  race that would otherwise make these missions flaky: the session that
  begins waiting first is deterministically the one whose
  `deadlock_timeout` fires first, and therefore the one that detects the
  cycle and cancels itself.

That last point is the rule for predicting the victim: **the first waiter
is the victim**, because it is the first to run the check.

## The tables

```sql
CREATE TABLE account (id int PRIMARY KEY, owner text NOT NULL,
                      balance numeric(12,2) NOT NULL);
-- 1 alice 100.00, 2 bob 200.00, 3 carol 300.00, 4 dave 400.00

CREATE TABLE ledger  (id serial PRIMARY KEY,
                      account_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES account(id),
                      delta numeric(12,2) NOT NULL, note text NOT NULL);

CREATE TABLE summary (id int PRIMARY KEY, total numeric(14,2) NOT NULL);
-- 1, 1000.00

CREATE TABLE tag     (name text PRIMARY KEY, uses int NOT NULL DEFAULT 0);
CREATE TABLE parent  (id int PRIMARY KEY);                       -- 1, 2
CREATE TABLE child   (id serial PRIMARY KEY,
                      parent_id int NOT NULL REFERENCES parent(id));
CREATE TABLE observation (label text PRIMARY KEY, value text NOT NULL);
```

## What the eight missions cover

Building the textbook deadlock; catching `40P01` and reading its message;
a deadlock made entirely of `INSERT`s; one that runs through a foreign
key; the canonical-order fix that removes it; measuring how long detection
costs; finding the cycle with `pg_blocking_pids` and `pg_locks` while it
is happening; and the lock upgrade that deadlocks on a single row. The
challenge builds a transfer that cannot deadlock and proves it with three
overlapping concurrent transfers. The review finds a cycle that spans two
tables and eliminates it.

# Reading - sql/v3d05_deadlocks

The reframing worth carrying: a deadlock is not an event, it is a
**property of your code that concurrency reveals**. The database found it
for you, at some cost, and told you exactly which two processes and which
tuple. Very few classes of bug come with that quality of report.

## Notes

**Every deadlock is an ordering disagreement.** If all code paths acquired
locks in one global order, no cycle could form — this is the same argument
as lock ordering in operating systems, and it has the same fix. When you
find a deadlock, do not ask "how do I retry this"; ask "which two paths
disagree, and what order should both use".

**You do not have to write a lock statement to take a lock.** `UPDATE`,
`DELETE`, `INSERT` against a unique index, and inserting a child row all
acquire locks. Three of this sector's four shapes involve no explicit
locking clause at all, which is why "we don't use `SELECT FOR UPDATE`
anywhere" is not a defence.

**The victim is chosen by timing, not by fairness.** Whichever backend's
`deadlock_timeout` fires first runs the check and cancels itself. There is
no priority, no age preference, and no way to nominate a victim. Both
sides therefore need a retry.

**Retries must be idempotent and jittered.** A deadlock retry re-runs a
transaction that partially executed and rolled back — safe, because the
rollback was complete. But retrying immediately against the same
contending peer often reproduces the cycle, so back off with jitter, and
cap the attempts.

**Deadlocks are a latency problem before they are a correctness problem.**
Detection costs `deadlock_timeout` on the victim and however long the
survivor waited. At the default one second, a handful of deadlocks per
second is enough to make a service look broken while every individual
transaction eventually succeeds.

**Batch statements deadlock too.** `UPDATE account SET … WHERE id IN
(3,1,2)` locks rows in whatever order the plan produces them — index
order, usually, but a sequential scan or a parallel plan may differ. Two
such statements with overlapping id sets can deadlock. Locking explicitly
in sorted order first is what makes a bulk update safe, and it is also why
`ORDER BY` on a locking `SELECT` is not decoration.

**A deadlock is not a data-integrity event.** The victim's transaction is
rolled back completely, exactly as if it had issued `ROLLBACK` itself. No
partial writes survive, no locks leak, and the survivor is unaffected. The
only lasting damage is the latency and the dead tuples the victim wrote —
which is why "we get a few deadlocks a day" is a performance report, not a
corruption report, and why the correct immediate response is a retry
rather than a data audit.

**Ordering must be derivable without coordination.** Ascending primary key
works because both sides compute the same order from the ids alone, with
no communication. An order that depends on which row you happened to read
first, or on the direction of a transfer, or on the planner's chosen scan,
is not an order — it only looks like one until the day the two paths
disagree.

**The lock order has to include the tables.** Once a workload touches more
than one table, the cycle can run between them, and no amount of
per-table discipline helps. This is the case the review mission is built
on, and the fix is a documented convention rather than anything the code
can enforce.

## ex1 — the textbook cycle

Two accounts, two transactions, opposite order. Predict the victim from
the rule above before you run it: the session that starts waiting first.

## ex2 — reading the report

Catching `40P01` in PL/pgSQL and recording `SQLERRM` gives you the
`DETAIL` text with both process ids and both transaction ids. That is the
same text your production log contains, and being able to parse it under
pressure is the point of the exercise.

## ex3 — deadlock by INSERT

No `UPDATE`, no locking clause. The second inserter of a duplicate key
waits on the first inserter's transaction to find out whether the key will
exist. Two loaders with overlapping key sets in different orders is a
real and very common production incident.

## ex4 — the cycle through a foreign key

The locks are on `parent`, but only one of the two statements in each
transaction mentions that table. This is the shape that survives code
review, because neither path looks like it touches what the other
touches.

## ex5 — the fix

`least()` and `greatest()` give a canonical order for two rows without
any coordination. Run the same two transfers that deadlocked in ex1 and
watch both succeed. Note that the function still holds locks — it has not
become lock-free, it has become *ordered*.

## ex6 — what detection costs

Time the caught deadlock. It is at least `deadlock_timeout`, because
nothing looks for cycles until a wait has lasted that long. Lowering the
setting makes detection faster and the checks more frequent; it does not
make the cycle go away.

## ex7 — finding it live

`pg_blocking_pids(pid)` is the first query of any "everything is stuck"
incident. Alongside it, `pg_locks WHERE NOT granted` shows what kind of
lock is being waited for — and a row-lock wait appears as `transactionid`,
because you wait for the holding transaction to end.

## ex8 — the upgrade

One row, two share holders, two upgrade attempts. There is no ordering
mistake to fix here; the fix is to take `FOR UPDATE` at the start if you
might write.

## Further reading

- [Deadlocks](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/explicit-locking.html#LOCKING-DEADLOCKS) — the manual's advice, which is exactly "use a consistent order".
- [Error Reporting: log_lock_waits](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/runtime-config-logging.html) — turn it on before you need it.
- [pg_blocking_pids](https://www.postgresql.org/docs/16/functions-info.html) — and `pg_safe_snapshot_blocking_pids` for the SSI equivalent.
- [Advanced deadlock analysis](https://www.cybertec-postgresql.com/en/postgresql-understanding-deadlocks/) — worked examples of reading the DETAIL section.

# V3·D5 — Deadlocks: causes, logs, and write ordering (archive)

## Concepts

### Reading the report

```
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 4312 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8891;
         blocked by process 4287.
         Process 4287 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8894;
         blocked by process 4312.
HINT:  See server log for query details.
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,3) in relation "account"
```

Four things to extract, in order of usefulness:

1. **The relation and tuple in `CONTEXT`** — the row the victim was
   waiting for when it gave up. Half the diagnosis.
2. **The cycle in `DETAIL`** — one line per edge. Two lines is the common
   case; three or more means three or more transactions, which is rarer
   and almost always a batch job.
3. **The victim** — the process the error was raised in, which is the
   last one listed.
4. **The queries** — only in the server log, and only if
   `log_lock_waits = on` or the statements are logged by other means. Turn
   that on. Without it you have a tuple id and a guess.

### The settings

```sql
SHOW deadlock_timeout;        -- '1s' by default; detection latency
SHOW log_lock_waits;          -- turn on; logs waits longer than the above
SET  lock_timeout = '2s';     -- an independent cap; 55P03, not 40P01
```

`deadlock_timeout` is superuser-settable only. Lowering it to, say, 200ms
makes the wait-graph check run more often on every waiting backend — worth
it on a system where deadlocks are frequent and latency matters, wasteful
otherwise.

### Canonical ordering, three ways

```sql
-- two known rows
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = least(a, b)    FOR UPDATE;
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = greatest(a, b) FOR UPDATE;

-- a set of rows, one statement
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = ANY(p_ids) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;

-- across tables: pick an order and document it
--   1. summary   2. account   3. ledger
```

The cross-table rule is the one that gets forgotten. Write it in a comment
at the top of the module, because there is nothing in the code that
enforces it.

### The retry, on the client

```python
for attempt in range(5):
    try:
        with conn.transaction():
            transfer(conn, a, b, amount)
        break
    except (DeadlockDetected, SerializationFailure):
        conn.rollback()
        time.sleep(random.uniform(0, 0.05 * 2 ** attempt))
```

`40P01` and `40001` get the same handler: both mean "your transaction was
rolled back cleanly, try again". The rollback is complete, so a retry is
safe as long as the transaction has no side effects outside the database.

### The four shapes, side by side

```sql
-- 1. opposite update order
-- A: UPDATE account WHERE id = 1;  then  id = 2
-- B: UPDATE account WHERE id = 2;  then  id = 1

-- 2. unique-index insertion (no locking clause anywhere)
-- A: INSERT INTO tag VALUES ('alpha'); then ('beta')
-- B: INSERT INTO tag VALUES ('beta');  then ('alpha')

-- 3. foreign key (the cycle runs through a table neither INSERT names)
-- A: SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
--    INSERT INTO child (parent_id) VALUES (2);
-- B: SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE;
--    INSERT INTO child (parent_id) VALUES (1);

-- 4. lock upgrade (one row, no ordering mistake possible)
-- A: SELECT ... id = 3 FOR SHARE;  then  FOR UPDATE
-- B: SELECT ... id = 3 FOR SHARE;  then  FOR UPDATE
```

Shapes 1, 2 and 3 are ordering bugs and have an ordering fix. Shape 4 is a
strength bug: take `FOR UPDATE` on the first read if you might write.

### Finding it while it happens

```sql
SELECT a.pid,
       a.state,
       a.wait_event_type || '/' || a.wait_event AS waiting,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)                  AS blocked_by,
       now() - a.xact_start                     AS txn_age,
       left(a.query, 60)                        AS q
  FROM pg_stat_activity a
 WHERE a.backend_type = 'client backend'
 ORDER BY cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) DESC, txn_age DESC;
```

`Lock/transactionid` means waiting for another transaction to end — the
presentation of row locks, unique-index conflicts and foreign key checks
alike. `Lock/tuple` means queueing behind other waiters for one row.
`Lock/relation` means a table-level lock, which almost always means DDL
somebody did not expect to be running.

Follow `blocked_by` transitively to the root. In a real incident the root
is frequently a session in state `idle in transaction`, which is sector
D8's subject.

## Common mistakes

1. **Treating a deadlock as a database problem.** It is an ordering bug in
   your code that the database detected for free.
2. **Retrying without fixing the order.** Works, costs `deadlock_timeout`
   per attempt, and gets worse under load rather than better.
3. **Assuming you are safe because you never write `FOR UPDATE`.**
   `UPDATE`, `DELETE`, duplicate-key `INSERT` and child-row `INSERT` all
   take locks.
4. **Ordering within one table but not across tables.** The cycle simply
   moves.
5. **Believing a higher isolation level helps.** `SERIALIZABLE` adds
   40001s; the lock cycle is unchanged.
6. **Relying on `IN (...)` order.** `WHERE id IN (3,1,2)` locks in plan
   order, not in list order.
7. **No jitter in the retry.** Two contending clients retry in lockstep
   and reproduce the cycle.
8. **`log_lock_waits` off in production.** You get a tuple id and no
   query, and the incident becomes archaeology.

## The interview answer

> *"You are seeing deadlocks in production. Walk me through it."*

First, confirm the shape from the log: the `DETAIL` gives me both process
ids and the wait edges, and the `CONTEXT` gives me the relation and tuple
the victim was blocked on. With `log_lock_waits` on I also get the
statements. Then I look for two code paths that touch the same rows in
different orders — including implicit locks from `UPDATE`, duplicate-key
`INSERT`, and foreign key checks, since most deadlocks involve no explicit
locking clause. The fix is a canonical acquisition order, usually
ascending primary key, applied by every path and extended across tables if
the cycle spans them; for two rows that is `least`/`greatest`, for many it
is a locking `SELECT ... ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE` taken up front. I keep a
jittered retry on `40P01` regardless, because ordering fixes the ones I
know about. And I check `deadlock_timeout`, because every deadlock costs
at least that much latency on both sides — a system with frequent
deadlocks is slow long before it is incorrect.

### Two settings to change before you need them

```
deadlock_timeout = 1s        # detection latency; superuser-only
log_lock_waits   = on        # logs every wait longer than the above
log_line_prefix  = '%m [%p] %a %u@%d '   # pid and application_name in every line
```

The prefix matters as much as the rest: the deadlock `DETAIL` names
process ids, and without `%p` and `%a` in the prefix you cannot match
those ids to the statements logged around them. Set `application_name` per
service and the report tells you which two components disagreed.

## Check yourself

1. What SQLSTATE is a deadlock, and what SQLSTATE is a serialization
   failure?
2. Which process is chosen as the victim, and on what basis?
3. What does `ShareLock on transaction 8891` mean you are waiting for?
4. Give three ways to acquire a lock without writing a locking clause.
5. Why can two `INSERT`s deadlock?
6. How long does a deadlock take to detect, and what controls it?
7. Why does `SERIALIZABLE` not prevent deadlocks?
8. Write the two statements that make a two-account transfer
   order-safe.
9. Why is `WHERE id IN (3,1,2)` not a lock order?
10. Your cycle runs through `parent` but neither statement mentions
    `parent`. What is happening?
11. What does `pg_blocking_pids(pid)` return, and when do you reach for
    it?
12. After a deadlock, is a retry of the whole transaction safe? What
    would make it unsafe?
lessons.fullReading:
# Long read — ordering is the only real fix

Deadlock is one of the oldest results in systems: Coffman, Elphick and
Shoshani set out the four necessary conditions in 1971 — mutual exclusion,
hold-and-wait, no preemption, and circular wait. A system that breaks any
one of them cannot deadlock. Databases keep the first three on purpose:
locks are exclusive by design, transactions hold locks while acquiring
more, and locks are not taken away because doing so would break
atomicity.

That leaves circular wait, which is why every practical answer to deadlock
in every system — kernels, distributed locks, PostgreSQL — is the same:
impose a total order on lock acquisition. Everything else is detection and
recovery, which is what the database does *for* you and what your code
should not need.

## Why PostgreSQL detects instead of preventing

There are two families of strategy. **Prevention** schemes like wound-wait
and wait-die use transaction timestamps to decide, at wait time, whether
to allow the wait or abort somebody immediately. They never build a cycle
but they abort transactions that would have been fine. **Detection**
waits, notices the cycle, and aborts exactly one participant.

PostgreSQL detects, and it detects lazily: nothing looks for a cycle until
some backend has waited `deadlock_timeout`. The reasoning is economic.
Almost all lock waits are short and legitimate, walking the wait graph
takes a lock on shared memory, and doing it on every wait would tax the
common case to speed up the rare one. One second of latency for a genuine
deadlock is a good price for zero overhead on the millions of waits that
resolve normally. Some distributed systems — including CockroachDB and
Spanner, which cannot cheaply build a global wait graph — choose
prevention instead, and pay for it in spurious aborts.

## The shapes nobody sees coming

**Indexes.** Two transactions inserting into the same B-tree page can
briefly conflict, and unique-index enforcement makes a duplicate inserter
wait on the first inserter's transaction id. A bulk load that inserts the
same set of keys from two workers in different orders deadlocks with no
`UPDATE` anywhere.

**Foreign keys.** The parent-row lock is taken by the child insert, so a
cycle can run through a table your statement never names. Since 9.3 this
is much rarer, because the lock is `FOR KEY SHARE` and no longer conflicts
with ordinary parent updates — but it still conflicts with `FOR UPDATE`,
which is why "lock the parent to be safe" is such an expensive habit.

**Triggers.** A trigger writes rows you did not write, in an order you did
not choose, inside your transaction. Two tables with triggers that update
each other's summary rows is a deadlock generator, and the statement in
the log will be the innocent one.

**`ON CONFLICT`.** Upsert takes a speculative insertion token and can wait
on another inserter of the same key. Two batch upserts with overlapping
keys in different orders deadlock, which is why sorting the rows of a bulk
upsert by key is standard practice — sector D6 returns to this.

**Parallel plans and bulk updates.** `UPDATE … WHERE id IN (…)` locks in
plan order. Change the statistics and the plan flips from index scan to
sequential scan, the lock order changes, and a system that ran for two
years starts deadlocking after an `ANALYZE`. This is a genuinely
unpleasant class of incident and the reason to lock explicitly, in an
ordered statement, before a bulk write.

## Table-level locks, and the deadlock nobody expects

Everything above is about row locks, but PostgreSQL's heavyweight lock
manager also handles table locks, and those produce a distinctive and
particularly disruptive class of deadlock.

`ALTER TABLE`, `DROP INDEX`, `TRUNCATE` and `VACUUM FULL` take
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE`, which conflicts with everything including plain
`SELECT`. A migration that begins by reading a table (taking
`ACCESS SHARE`) and then alters it has *upgraded* a table lock, and if a
concurrent session does the reverse the two deadlock at the relation
level — with the whole table blocked behind each of them, since
`ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` requests queue and everything behind them queues too.

This is why the standard migration advice is to set `lock_timeout` before
any DDL:

```sql
SET lock_timeout = '3s';
ALTER TABLE orders ADD COLUMN note text;
```

If the lock cannot be taken in three seconds, the migration fails
harmlessly and can be retried; without it, one long-running `SELECT` turns
a metadata change into a total outage while every subsequent query piles
up behind the pending `ACCESS EXCLUSIVE` request. The lock is fast to
*hold* — adding a nullable column is instant since PostgreSQL 11 — and
potentially very slow to *acquire*, and those two facts are routinely
confused.

## Performance notes

Deadlocks are expensive in three places. The victim pays
`deadlock_timeout` plus the cost of everything it had done. The survivor
pays whatever it waited. And the whole system pays for the wait-graph
checks, which take an exclusive lock on the lock manager's partitions —
noticeable when many backends are waiting at once.

The counter to watch is `pg_stat_database.deadlocks`. A steady non-zero
rate is a design signal, not noise. Correlate it with a latency
percentile: deadlock-heavy systems usually show a p99 pinned suspiciously
close to a multiple of `deadlock_timeout`, which is the fingerprint.

There is also a subtler cost: the retry. If a retried transaction is long,
you re-run all of it, and under contention the retry can deadlock again.
Shortening transactions helps deadlocks the same way it helps everything
else in this volume — a transaction that holds locks for ten milliseconds
is very hard to catch in a cycle.

## The retry is not optional

Even with a perfect lock order, keep the retry. Ordering fixes the cycles
you know about; a new code path, a new trigger, or a foreign key added
next quarter can introduce one you do not. A jittered retry on `40P01`
turns that from an error the user sees into a few milliseconds nobody
notices, and it costs a dozen lines.

The two properties that make a retry correct are worth restating, because
they are the same two that make queue handlers correct in D4 and upserts
correct in D6. First, the transaction must have no side effects outside
the database — a retried transaction that already sent an email sends it
twice. Second, it must re-run from the beginning, including the reads: the
values it read the first time came from a transaction that no longer
exists, and reusing them reintroduces the lost update.

## When ordering is not available

Occasionally the lock order genuinely cannot be known in advance: the rows
to lock depend on data read while already holding locks. Three options,
in order of preference.

**Restructure so it can.** Compute the full set of keys first, sort, lock
in one ordered statement, then do the work. This is almost always
possible and almost always the right answer.

**Use a coarser lock.** One advisory lock — sector D7 — around the whole
operation removes the cycle by removing the concurrency. If the operation
is rare (a nightly rebalance, a migration), that is a fine trade.

**Fail fast and retry.** `SET lock_timeout` to something small so a
contending path gives up before the deadlock detector has to, and retry
with backoff. This turns 40P01 into 55P03, which is not obviously better,
but it does cap the latency at a number you chose rather than at
`deadlock_timeout`.

What you should not do is lower `deadlock_timeout` globally and call it
fixed. Faster detection of a bug is not the absence of a bug, and the
extra wait-graph traffic is paid by every backend that ever waits.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 1 — the textbook deadlock

Edit `ex1/solution.sql`. Two transfers in opposite directions, each
touching the same two accounts in the order its own business logic
suggests.

```
-- @A                    BEGIN;
--                       UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10
--                        WHERE id = 1;
-- @B                    BEGIN;
--                       UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10
--                        WHERE id = 2;
-- @B async expect 40P01 UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10
--                        WHERE id = 1;          -- waits for A
-- @A                    UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10
--                        WHERE id = 2;          -- waits for B: cycle
--                       COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A                    record 'alice' = account 1's balance   (expect 90.00)
--                       record 'bob'   = account 2's balance   (expect 210.00)
```

Neither transaction did anything unusual. A debits 1 and credits 2; B
debits 2 and credits 1. Each holds what the other wants next.

B is the victim, and you can predict that: B starts waiting first, so B's
`deadlock_timeout` fires first, B walks the wait graph, finds itself in a
cycle, and cancels itself with `40P01`. A's wait then resolves and A
commits normally — which is why the final balances are A's transfer only.

Note that `expect` and `async` combine on one marker line, and that an
async block's expectation is checked at `-- @join`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Draw the wait graph as two arrows before you run anything. A holds row 1
and wants row 2; B holds row 2 and wants row 1. Two arrows, one loop.

## Hint 2
Note that no locking clause appears anywhere in this file. A plain

```sql
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
```

takes `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` on that row and holds it until the transaction
ends. "We do not use `SELECT FOR UPDATE`" is not a defence against
deadlocks.

## Hint 3
Six blocks. A's second block contains both the blocking `UPDATE` and the
`COMMIT`; it will sit waiting for roughly a second while the detector
does its work, then proceed. `-- @join` goes after it, before the
observations.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Predict the balances for the *other* outcome as well — if A had been the
victim, they would be 110.00 and 190.00. Both are legitimate; only the
timing of the two `deadlock_timeout` timers decides. That is why both
sides of a deadlock-prone pair need a retry.

## Hint 2
The message the victim receives, in full, is worth reading once:

```
ERROR:  deadlock detected
DETAIL:  Process 4312 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8891;
         blocked by process 4287. ...
CONTEXT:  while updating tuple (0,1) in relation "account"
```

`ShareLock on transaction N` is what waiting for a row lock looks like —
you wait for the *holder's transaction* to end, not for the row.

## Hint 3
If nothing deadlocks and both blocks succeed, the two transactions
probably touched the accounts in the same order. Check that A's pair is
(1 then 2) and B's is (2 then 1) — a cycle needs disagreement.

exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 2 — catch it and read what it says

Edit `ex2/solution.sql`. The same cycle as ex1, but B catches the error
instead of dying, so you can capture the report.

B's second block is `async` and contains a `DO` block that performs the
conflicting update, catches `deadlock_detected`, and records three things
before committing:

| label              | value                                        |
|--------------------|----------------------------------------------|
| `dl_sqlstate`      | `SQLSTATE` inside the handler                |
| `dl_mentions_process` | whether `SQLERRM` contains the text `Process` |
| `dl_relation`      | the literal text `account`                   |

```
-- @A        BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
-- @B        BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 2;
-- @B async  DO $$ ... UPDATE ... id = 1 ... EXCEPTION WHEN deadlock_detected
--                THEN record ... END $$;
--           COMMIT;
-- @A        UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2;
--           COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'total' = sum(balance) over all accounts   (expect 1000.00)
```

Expected: `dl_sqlstate` = `40P01`, `dl_mentions_process` = `true`.

Two things are being demonstrated. The handler works — a deadlock is
catchable like any other error, and because the `DO` block's `BEGIN ...
EXCEPTION` is a subtransaction, B's transaction survives and commits its
first `UPDATE`. And the message is *evidence*: `SQLERRM` carries the same
`DETAIL` text your production log gets, naming both processes and both
transaction ids.

Since B now commits its debit and A commits its whole transfer, the total
across all four accounts still has to be 1000.00 — money is conserved even
through a deadlock, because the victim statement's work was rolled back
completely.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex2`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask what state B's transaction is in inside the handler. The failed
statement was rolled back to the subtransaction's savepoint, so B is
healthy and may write — which is the only reason recording the message is
possible at all.

## Hint 2
Testing a substring in SQL:

```sql
INSERT INTO observation (label, value)
VALUES ('dl_mentions_process', (SQLERRM LIKE '%Process%')::text);
```

`SQLERRM` holds the primary message plus the detail; `SQLSTATE` holds
`40P01`.

## Hint 3
B's async block must contain the `DO` **and** the `COMMIT`, because A's
next block waits on B's row-2 lock and that lock is only released at B's
commit. Leave the `COMMIT` out and A's block waits until the gate's
`lock_timeout` kills it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Consider whether catching a deadlock is a good idea in real code. It
usually is not: the transaction has lost the work that statement did, and
carrying on as though nothing happened commits a partial result. Catch it
at the *edge*, roll back the whole transaction, and retry. This exercise
catches it only to read it.

## Hint 2
For the full picture in production you want the server log, not the
client:

```
log_lock_waits = on
deadlock_timeout = 1s
log_line_prefix = '%m [%p] %a %u@%d '
```

`log_lock_waits` also logs *near*-deadlocks — any wait longer than
`deadlock_timeout` — which is how you find the ordering bug before it
becomes an incident.

## Hint 3
If `dl_sqlstate` is missing entirely, the handler never fired: either no
deadlock occurred, or you caught `WHEN OTHERS` somewhere above it. The
condition name is `deadlock_detected`.

exercises.title: Ex3
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 3 — a deadlock made only of INSERTs

Edit `ex3/solution.sql`. No `UPDATE`, no `DELETE`, no locking clause. Two
loaders inserting the same two tags in opposite orders.

```
-- @A                    BEGIN; INSERT INTO tag (name) VALUES ('alpha');
-- @B                    BEGIN; INSERT INTO tag (name) VALUES ('beta');
-- @B async expect 40P01 INSERT INTO tag (name) VALUES ('alpha');
-- @A                    INSERT INTO tag (name) VALUES ('beta');
--                       COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A                    record 'tags' = string_agg(name, ',' ORDER BY name)
--                       record 'tag_count' = count(*)
```

Expected: `tags` = `alpha,beta`, `tag_count` = `2`.

`tag.name` is a primary key. When B inserts `'alpha'`, the unique index
already holds an entry for it — inserted by A, not yet committed. B cannot
decide whether that is a duplicate until A's fate is known, so it waits on
A's transaction id. A then waits on B's for `'beta'`, and the cycle is
complete.

This is the shape that catches teams who believe deadlocks are about
explicit locking. Two importers, two overlapping key sets, no coordination
about the order rows are processed in — and the fix is a single `ORDER BY`
in whatever produces the batch.

Note also that B's rolled-back insert leaves a **dead tuple** and consumes
a value from any sequence involved. Failed inserts are not free.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex3`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Ask what B is waiting for when it inserts a key A has already inserted but
not committed. It cannot report a duplicate (A might roll back) and it
cannot proceed (A might commit). Its only option is to wait for A to
finish.

## Hint 2
This is the same wait as a row lock, and it looks identical in the logs:

```
Process 4312 waits for ShareLock on transaction 8891
```

`ShareLock on transaction N` — waiting for a transaction to end — is how
unique-index conflicts, row locks and foreign key checks all present
themselves.

## Hint 3
Six blocks, the same skeleton as ex1 with `INSERT` in place of `UPDATE`.
A's second block must contain the `COMMIT` so the tags actually persist;
B's transaction is rolled back by the gate after the expected failure, so
neither of B's inserts survives.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Work out the one-line fix for a real loader. If both importers sorted
their batch — `ORDER BY name` — before inserting, they would take the keys
in the same order and no cycle could form. Sorting a batch before writing
it is the cheapest deadlock prevention there is.

## Hint 2
`INSERT ... ON CONFLICT DO NOTHING` does **not** avoid this. The
speculative-insertion machinery still has to wait on the other inserter to
learn whether there is a conflict, so two upserts with overlapping keys in
different orders deadlock exactly the same way. Sector D6 returns to it.

## Hint 3
If both inserts succeed with no deadlock, check that B's second insert
really names the key A inserted first. `'alpha'` in both A's first block
and B's async block is what creates the first edge.

exercises.title: Ex4
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 4 — the cycle that runs through a foreign key

Edit `ex4/solution.sql`. The hardest shape to spot in review, because
neither transaction looks like it touches what the other touches.

`child.parent_id` references `parent(id)`, and `parent` holds ids 1 and 2.

```
-- @A                    BEGIN;
--                       SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = 1 FOR UPDATE;
-- @B                    BEGIN;
--                       SELECT * FROM parent WHERE id = 2 FOR UPDATE;
-- @B async expect 40P01 INSERT INTO child (parent_id) VALUES (1);
-- @A                    INSERT INTO child (parent_id) VALUES (2);
--                       COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A                    record 'children' = count(*) FROM child   (expect 1)
--                       record 'child_parent' = the surviving row's parent_id
```

Expected: `children` = `1`, `child_parent` = `2`.

The `INSERT`s never mention `parent`, yet each one needs `FOR KEY SHARE`
on the parent row to guarantee it will still exist at commit — and `FOR
KEY SHARE` conflicts with the other session's `FOR UPDATE`. The cycle runs
entirely through rows in a table neither `INSERT` names.

There are two lessons. Explicit `FOR UPDATE` on a parent row is far more
expensive than it looks: it blocks every child insert, everywhere. And a
canonical lock order has to cover *tables*, not just rows — "always lock
parents in ascending id order" would have prevented this, and no amount of
care inside either transaction alone would.

Had A and B used `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` instead — which is what a plain
`UPDATE parent SET name = ...` takes — there would be no conflict at all.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex4`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
List the locks each transaction holds and wants, naming the table each
lock is on. Both lists mention `parent`, even though only two of the four
statements do.

## Hint 2
The lock an insert takes on its parent is the weakest one that does the
job:

```sql
-- what INSERT INTO child (parent_id) VALUES (1) effectively does first
SELECT 1 FROM parent WHERE id = 1 FOR KEY SHARE;
```

Compatible with `FOR NO KEY UPDATE`, conflicts with `FOR UPDATE`. That
distinction is the whole exercise.

## Hint 3
Six blocks, same skeleton as ex1 and ex3. The observation of
`child_parent` needs a query over the single surviving row: `SELECT
parent_id::text FROM child` returns one row after B is rolled back.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Try the variant where A and B use `FOR NO KEY UPDATE` instead of `FOR
UPDATE` and predict the result first. No conflict, no cycle, both
transactions commit — which is precisely why PostgreSQL 9.3 introduced the
weaker mode, and why reaching for `FOR UPDATE` by reflex is a real cost.

## Hint 2
The general form of this bug does not need an explicit lock at all.
Triggers produce it constantly: a trigger on `child` that updates a
counter on `parent` writes rows your statement never named, in an order
you never chose. When a deadlock report names a table your code does not
mention, look for foreign keys and triggers first.

## Hint 3
If nothing deadlocks, check that A locks parent 1 while B locks parent 2,
and that the inserts are crossed — A inserts a child of 2, B a child of 1.
Uncrossed inserts produce two happy transactions.

exercises.title: Ex5
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 5 — remove the cycle with a canonical order

Edit `ex5/solution.sql`. Run ex1's schedule again, with one change: a
function that always acquires the two account rows in ascending id order,
whichever direction the money is going.

Write

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION transfer(p_from int, p_to int, p_amt numeric)
RETURNS void LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ ... $$;
```

which:

1. locks `account` id `least(p_from, p_to)` with `FOR UPDATE`;
2. locks `account` id `greatest(p_from, p_to)` with `FOR UPDATE`;
3. subtracts `p_amt` from `p_from` and adds it to `p_to`.

Then the interleaving:

```
-- @A async  BEGIN; SELECT transfer(1, 2, 10); COMMIT;
-- @B        BEGIN; SELECT transfer(2, 1, 20); COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'alice' = account 1's balance     (expect 110.00)
--           record 'bob'   = account 2's balance     (expect 190.00)
--           record 'total' = sum(balance)            (expect 1000.00)
```

Both transfers succeed. B may wait for A, but it waits for *both* locks in
the same order A took them, so there is no cycle to form — a waiter that
holds nothing the holder wants can only wait, never deadlock.

Note what has not changed: the function still takes exclusive row locks
and still serialises the two transfers. Ordering does not remove
contention; it removes the *cycle*. That is the trade, and it is almost
always the right one, because a wait ends in milliseconds while a deadlock
costs `deadlock_timeout` plus a retry.

`least()` and `greatest()` are the two-row form. For a set of rows the
equivalent is one statement: `SELECT 1 FROM account WHERE id = ANY(p_ids)
ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex5`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The rule to encode is "the lock order must not depend on the direction of
the transfer". Anything derived only from the two ids — smallest first,
largest first, alphabetical by owner — works, as long as every caller uses
the same one.

## Hint 2
Locking without needing the row's contents:

```sql
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = least(p_from, p_to) FOR UPDATE;
```

`PERFORM` runs the query and discards the result; the lock is held by the
calling transaction until it ends, not until the function returns.

## Hint 3
Four statements in the body: two `PERFORM`s and two `UPDATE`s. The
`UPDATE`s may go in any order — once both rows are locked, nothing can
interleave between them.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask why `PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id IN (p_from, p_to) FOR UPDATE`
without an `ORDER BY` is not good enough. The rows are locked in the order
the plan produces them, which is index order today and could be sequential
scan order after the table grows. A lock order that depends on the planner
is not a lock order.

## Hint 2
The same discipline written as a single ordered statement, which is what
you want for more than two rows:

```sql
PERFORM 1 FROM account WHERE id = ANY(p_ids) ORDER BY id FOR UPDATE;
```

The `LockRows` node sits above the `Sort`, so rows really are locked in
sorted order — worth confirming with `EXPLAIN` the first time you rely
on it.

## Hint 3
If the two blocks still deadlock, the function is probably locking
`p_from` then `p_to` rather than smallest then largest. Print
`least(p_from, p_to)` for both call directions and check they agree.

exercises.title: Ex6
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 6 — what detection costs

Edit `ex6/solution.sql`. Deadlocks are a latency problem before they are a
correctness problem. Measure it.

Reproduce ex1's cycle, but have B time its own wait: capture
`clock_timestamp()` before the conflicting statement, and in the
`deadlock_detected` handler record how many milliseconds elapsed, plus the
current `deadlock_timeout` setting.

```
-- @A        BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 1;
-- @B        BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 2;
-- @B async  DO $$ DECLARE t0 timestamptz := clock_timestamp(); BEGIN
--             UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 1;
--           EXCEPTION WHEN deadlock_detected THEN
--             record 'detect_ms' = elapsed milliseconds, as an integer
--             record 'dl_timeout' = current_setting('deadlock_timeout')
--           END $$;
--           COMMIT;
-- @A        UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 10 WHERE id = 2; COMMIT;
-- @join
```

Expected: `dl_timeout` = `1s`, and `detect_ms` at least 900.

Use `clock_timestamp()`, not `now()`. `now()` is the transaction's start
time and never moves inside a transaction, so it would report zero — which
is a useful thing to get wrong once.

Nothing looks for a cycle until some backend has waited a full
`deadlock_timeout`. That is a deliberate economic choice: almost every
lock wait is short and legitimate, and walking the wait graph takes a lock
on shared memory, so charging every wait for the rare case would be a bad
trade. The consequence for you is that a system doing a handful of
deadlocks per second has a p99 latency pinned near a multiple of one
second while every individual transaction eventually succeeds.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex6`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Predict the number before running. It cannot be much below
`deadlock_timeout`, because that is when the check first happens, and it
should not be much above it, because the check finds the cycle
immediately.

## Hint 2
Elapsed milliseconds as an integer:

```sql
(extract(epoch FROM clock_timestamp() - t0) * 1000)::int::text
```

`extract(epoch ...)` from an interval gives seconds as a double.

## Hint 3
Declare `t0 timestamptz := clock_timestamp();` in the `DO` block's
`DECLARE` section so it is evaluated before the `UPDATE` runs. Both
observations belong inside the handler, since that is the only place the
elapsed time is meaningful.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what lowering `deadlock_timeout` to 100ms would buy and cost. Faster
detection, so lower tail latency — and a wait-graph check on every backend
that waits longer than 100ms, which on a busy system is many of them. It
is a throughput trade, and it is not a fix for the ordering bug.

## Hint 2
The setting you actually want first is the one that finds the bug before
it becomes a deadlock:

```
log_lock_waits = on
```

It logs every wait longer than `deadlock_timeout`, with the blocking pid.
Near-deadlocks show up as a steady trickle in the log long before the
first real cycle.

## Hint 3
If `detect_ms` comes back as `0`, you used `now()` instead of
`clock_timestamp()`. If it comes back around 5000, the gate's
`lock_timeout` fired instead of the deadlock detector — check that both
transactions really hold a row the other wants.

exercises.title: Ex7
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 7 — finding the wait while it is happening

Edit `ex7/solution.sql`. No deadlock this time — just an ordinary block,
observed from the outside with the two queries you will reach for in every
"everything is stuck" incident.

```
-- @B        SET application_name = 'session_b';
-- @A        BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 3;
-- @B async  BEGIN; UPDATE account SET balance = balance - 10 WHERE id = 3;
--           COMMIT;
-- @A        record 'b_blocked'      = does B have any blocking pids? (true)
--           record 'b_blocked_by_a' = is A's pid among them?         (true)
--           record 'b_wait_event'   = B's wait_event_type || '/' || wait_event
--           record 'waits_on_xid'   = is there an ungranted lock of
--                                     locktype 'transactionid'?      (true)
--           COMMIT;
-- @join
```

Expected: `b_blocked` = `true`, `b_blocked_by_a` = `true`, `b_wait_event`
= `Lock/transactionid`, `waits_on_xid` = `true`.

Find B by `application_name`, and A by `pg_backend_pid()`:

```sql
SELECT cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(pid)) > 0
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE application_name = 'session_b';

SELECT pg_backend_pid() = ANY(pg_blocking_pids(pid))
  FROM pg_stat_activity WHERE application_name = 'session_b';
```

`pg_blocking_pids(pid)` is the single most useful function in this
sector: hand it a process id, get back the processes it is waiting on.
Chase it transitively and you have the wait graph the deadlock detector
walks.

The `wait_event` is worth memorising: `Lock/transactionid` means "waiting
for another transaction to end", which is what every row-lock,
unique-index and foreign-key wait looks like. `Lock/tuple` means queueing
behind other waiters for the same row, and `Lock/relation` means a table
lock — usually a DDL statement nobody expected to be running.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex7`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
A is the holder, not the waiter, so A is free to run queries while B is
stuck. That asymmetry is why you can always diagnose a block from a third
connection — or, here, from the blocking one.

## Hint 2
The ungranted-lock query:

```sql
SELECT EXISTS (
  SELECT 1 FROM pg_locks WHERE NOT granted AND locktype = 'transactionid'
)::text;
```

`pg_locks` shows both granted and pending entries; `NOT granted` is the
wait list.

## Hint 3
Six blocks. B's `SET application_name` must be its own block *before* A
takes the lock, and B's async block needs `BEGIN`, the `UPDATE` and
`COMMIT` together — A's observations run while B is inside that block,
and A's `COMMIT` is what finally releases it.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Follow the chain by hand: `pg_blocking_pids` on B gives A; on A it gives
an empty array, so A is the root. In a real incident the chain is often
five deep and the root is a session that is `idle in transaction` — which
is sector D8's entire subject.

## Hint 2
The full triage query, worth keeping in a snippet file:

```sql
SELECT a.pid, a.state, a.wait_event_type || '/' || a.wait_event AS waiting,
       pg_blocking_pids(a.pid) AS blocked_by,
       now() - a.xact_start AS txn_age, left(a.query, 60) AS q
  FROM pg_stat_activity a
 WHERE a.backend_type = 'client backend'
 ORDER BY cardinality(pg_blocking_pids(a.pid)) DESC, txn_age DESC;
```

## Hint 3
If `b_wait_event` comes back NULL, A's observation block ran before B had
started waiting. The gate holds the next block until an async session is
blocked or finished, so this should not happen — but if you moved the
`SET application_name` into the async block, B cannot be found by name and
the query returns no rows at all.

exercises.title: Ex8
exercises.prompt:
## Exercise 8 — one row, no ordering mistake, still a deadlock

Edit `ex8/solution.sql`. The lock upgrade, promised in D4.

Both sessions read the same row with `FOR SHARE` — a perfectly reasonable
"make sure this does not change while I decide" — and then both decide to
write it.

```
-- @A                    BEGIN;
--                       SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 3 FOR SHARE;
-- @B                    BEGIN;
--                       SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 3 FOR SHARE;
-- @B async expect 40P01 SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 3 FOR UPDATE;
-- @A                    SELECT * FROM account WHERE id = 3 FOR UPDATE;
--                       UPDATE account SET balance = balance + 5 WHERE id = 3;
--                       COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A                    record 'carol' = account 3's balance   (expect 305.00)
--                       record 'holders' = 'two share locks upgraded'
```

There is no acquisition order to fix. Both sessions touched one row, in
the only order available. The cycle exists because each holds a lock the
other's upgrade conflicts with — `FOR UPDATE` conflicts with `FOR SHARE`,
including a `FOR SHARE` held by a session that also wants to upgrade.

The fix is not ordering, it is **strength**: if there is any chance you
will write the row, take `FOR UPDATE` on the first read. The share lock
bought you nothing here — you were going to write anyway — and cost you a
deadlock.

Try the fixed version locally afterwards: change both `FOR SHARE`s to `FOR
UPDATE` and watch B simply wait for A and then proceed. Same contention,
no cycle.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks ex8`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
Write out who holds what. Both hold `FOR SHARE` on row 3. Both want `FOR
UPDATE` on row 3. Consult D4's compatibility matrix for whether `FOR
UPDATE` conflicts with `FOR SHARE`, and the cycle is immediate.

## Hint 2
The pattern in application code usually looks innocent:

```sql
SELECT balance FROM account WHERE id = $1 FOR SHARE;   -- "just checking"
-- ... a branch in the application ...
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + $2 WHERE id = $1;
```

The `UPDATE` is the upgrade. It does not look like a lock statement, which
is why this shape survives review.

## Hint 3
Six blocks. A's second block does three things: the upgrade, the actual
update, and the commit. Keep them together — splitting them adds nothing
and gives the gate another place to wait.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Notice that this is one of the two deadlock shapes with no ordering fix at
all; the other is a self-inflicted one involving triggers writing rows in
data-dependent order. When you cannot order, you must either take the
strong lock up front or reduce the concurrency, and the first is nearly
always cheaper.

## Hint 2
`xmax` on that row while both share locks are held is not a transaction id
at all — it is a **multixact** id, because one field has to encode two
holders. That is also why heavy `FOR SHARE` traffic has its own wraparound
risk and its own SLRU contention, entirely separate from ordinary
transaction ids.

## Hint 3
If no deadlock occurs, check that both sessions took `FOR SHARE` on the
*same* row before either tried to upgrade — two share locks on different
rows produce two happy transactions.

exercises.title: Challenge
exercises.prompt:
## Challenge — three transfers in a cycle, and none of them deadlock

Edit `challenge/solution.sql`. The real test of a lock order is a
*cyclic* workload: 1→2, 2→3, 3→1, all at once. Under any per-transfer
ordering ("lock the source, then the destination") this deadlocks
immediately. Under a canonical ordering it cannot.

Write

```sql
CREATE OR REPLACE FUNCTION safe_transfer(p_from int, p_to int,
                                         p_amt numeric)
RETURNS boolean LANGUAGE plpgsql AS $$ ... $$;
```

which:

1. rejects `p_from = p_to` by returning `false` without writing;
2. locks both account rows with `FOR UPDATE` in **ascending id order**,
   regardless of the direction of the transfer;
3. returns `false` without writing if the source balance is below
   `p_amt`;
4. otherwise moves the money, writes two `ledger` rows (note
   `'xfer ' || p_from || '->' || p_to`, deltas `-p_amt` and `+p_amt`),
   and returns `true`.

Then run all three transfers concurrently:

```
-- @A async  BEGIN; SELECT safe_transfer(1, 2, 10); COMMIT;
-- @B async  BEGIN; SELECT safe_transfer(2, 3, 20); COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        BEGIN; SELECT safe_transfer(3, 1, 30); COMMIT;
-- @A        record 'alice'/'bob'/'carol' = balances
--           record 'total'      = sum(balance)        (expect 1000.00)
--           record 'ledger_rows' = count(*) FROM ledger  (expect 6)
--           record 'deadlocks'  = 'none'
```

Expected balances: alice 100 - 10 + 30 = 120.00, bob 200 + 10 - 20 =
190.00, carol 300 + 20 - 30 = 290.00, dave unchanged at 400.00.

Two invariants make this a real test rather than a demonstration. The
total must be exactly 1000.00 — money is neither created nor destroyed by
any interleaving. And there must be exactly six ledger rows — two per
successful transfer, no duplicates from a retry, no missing pair from a
half-applied transfer.

The `p_from = p_to` guard in step 1 is not defensive padding. Without it,
`least` and `greatest` return the same id and the function locks the same
row twice — harmless, but the transfer then adds and subtracts on one row
and quietly does nothing while returning `true`.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks challenge`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The ordering rule and the business rule are separate concerns. Lock first,
in an order derived only from the ids; *then* read balances and decide.
Doing it the other way round — read, decide, lock — reintroduces the lost
update from D3.

## Hint 2
Reading a balance after locking:

```sql
SELECT balance INTO src FROM account WHERE id = p_from;
IF src < p_amt THEN RETURN false; END IF;
```

No `FOR UPDATE` needed on this read — the row is already locked by the
`PERFORM` above, and the read sees the current version.

## Hint 3
Body shape: the self-transfer guard; two `PERFORM ... FOR UPDATE` using
`least` and `greatest`; a `SELECT ... INTO` for the source balance; the
sufficiency check; two `UPDATE`s; one `INSERT` with two `VALUES` rows into
`ledger`; `RETURN true`. Nine statements, no loops.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Convince yourself the cycle really is broken before running it. Transfer
3→1 wants rows 1 and 3; under ascending order it takes 1 first. Transfer
1→2 also takes 1 first. Two transactions that both want row 1 first can
queue, but the one that gets it never has to wait for the one that does
not — a waiter holding nothing the holder wants cannot close a cycle.

## Hint 2
The invariant check is the part worth stealing for your own code:

```sql
SELECT sum(balance) FROM account;                        -- must be constant
SELECT sum(delta)   FROM ledger;                         -- must be 0.00
```

A conserved quantity plus a ledger that sums to zero catches almost every
concurrency bug in a money system, and both are cheap enough to assert in
a test after every scenario.

## Hint 3
If `ledger_rows` comes back as 4, one transfer returned `false` — most
likely 2→3 ran before 1→2 and bob had only 200.00, which is still enough;
check the balance guard uses `<` rather than `<=` and compares against
`p_amt`, not against zero.

exercises.title: Review 1
exercises.prompt:
## Review 1 — a cycle that spans two tables

Edit `review1/solution.sql`. Every fix so far ordered rows within one
table. This one cannot: the cycle runs between `summary` and `account`,
and each path takes them in the order its own author found natural.

The broken pair, which you must **not** write:

```sql
-- deposit: touch the running total first, then the account
UPDATE summary SET total = total + amt WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + amt WHERE id = acc;

-- withdraw: touch the account first, then the running total
UPDATE account SET balance = balance - amt WHERE id = acc;
UPDATE summary SET total = total - amt WHERE id = 1;
```

Run concurrently, those deadlock: the deposit holds `summary` and wants
`account`, the withdrawal holds `account` and wants `summary`.

Write two functions, `deposit(p_acc int, p_amt numeric)` and
`withdraw(p_acc int, p_amt numeric)`, both `RETURNS void`, that do the
same work under one **cross-table** order: **`summary` first, then
`account`**, in both directions. Each also writes a `ledger` row with note
`'deposit'` or `'withdraw'` and the appropriate signed `delta`.

Then:

```
-- @A async  BEGIN; SELECT deposit(1, 50); COMMIT;
-- @B        BEGIN; SELECT withdraw(2, 50); COMMIT;
-- @join
-- @A        record 'alice'   = account 1's balance      (expect 150.00)
--           record 'bob'     = account 2's balance      (expect 150.00)
--           record 'total'   = summary.total            (expect 1000.00)
--           record 'accounts_total' = sum(account.balance) (expect 1000.00)
--           record 'ledger_rows' = count(*) FROM ledger (expect 2)
```

The ordering rule here is a decision, not a derivation: nothing in the
data says `summary` comes before `account`. Somebody has to choose, write
it down, and hold every path to it — which is why the comment at the top
of the file matters as much as the code.

Note also that `summary` is a single hot row. Ordering removes the
deadlock; it does not remove the fact that every deposit and withdrawal
now serialises behind one row. That is the cost of a running total, and
knowing it is the point of putting the two problems in one exercise.

Run: `uv run dojo test v3d05_deadlocks review1`
exercises.hints:
## Hint 1
The bug is not in either function. Each is internally sensible; they
disagree with each other. Fixing one path in isolation just moves which
pair of paths conflicts.

## Hint 2
Both functions have the same skeleton:

```sql
UPDATE summary SET total = total + <signed amt> WHERE id = 1;
UPDATE account SET balance = balance + <signed amt> WHERE id = p_acc;
INSERT INTO ledger (account_id, delta, note) VALUES (p_acc, <signed>, '...');
```

An `UPDATE` takes the lock, so the order of the two `UPDATE`s *is* the
lock order — no explicit locking clause is involved.

## Hint 3
`deposit` uses `+ p_amt` in both updates; `withdraw` uses `- p_amt` in
both. The ledger delta is positive for a deposit and negative for a
withdrawal, which is what makes `sum(delta)` a meaningful audit later.
exercises.importantHints:
## Hint 1
Ask what would have to be true for the ordering to be *derivable* rather
than chosen. If every path always touched both tables, alphabetical order
by table name would do. In real systems some paths touch only one, and the
order still has to be documented — a convention nobody wrote down is a
convention that will be broken by the next contributor.

## Hint 2
The alternative to a hot summary row is to stop maintaining one:

```sql
CREATE MATERIALIZED VIEW summary_mv AS SELECT sum(balance) FROM account;
```

or simply computing the total on demand. A running total updated by every
transaction is a deliberate trade of write throughput for read latency,
and it is worth re-asking whether the read is frequent enough to justify
it.

## Hint 3
If the two blocks deadlock, one function still touches `account` first.
Read both bodies side by side — the failure mode of this exercise is
fixing one path and believing you fixed the pair.
